Datadog keeps more of the dollar than its suppliers do. Roughly 11-16 cents of each Datadog revenue dollar reaches a hyperscaler as hosting-and-software cost, of which roughly 4-6 cents becomes hyperscaler operating profit at AWS's FY2025 segment margin, against 22-23 cents of non-GAAP operating profit Datadog keeps and about 30 cents it spends on research. The largest claim on the dollar is Datadog's own engineering.

Peers at the same layer, for reference: Dynatrace FY2026 total gross margin 82% with subscription at 85%, and Elastic FY2026 total 76% with subscription at 81%, against Datadog's 80.0% for FY2025 and 78.6% in Q2 2026. All three give the same explanation for the cost line — Dynatrace cites "increased cloud-based hosting costs of $35.1 million", Elastic "an increase of $20.6 million in cloud hosting costs" — but Datadog's FY2025 hosting increment of $149.8m is 4x Dynatrace's and 7x Elastic's on a revenue base 1.7x and 2.0x theirs. Datadog is absorbing disproportionately more hosting-cost growth per revenue dollar than either pure-play peer, and only Dynatrace's subscription line moves in the same direction.▪

5.2 The marketplace channel cannot explain the gross-margin decline

AWS publishes its listing fees: 3.0% on public offers and private offers below $1m of contract value, 2.0% between $1m and $10m, 1.5% at $10m or more, and 1.5% on all renewals [docs.aws.amazon.com, accessed 2026-08-10] [web]. Channel-influenced ARR was 15% of total at December 2025, up from 4% in 2020 [deck: Investor Day 2026, 2026-02-12, slide 137]. Datadog's marketplace volume concentrates in large private offers and renewals, so the applicable rate is 1.5-2.0% for most transacted dollars. The ceiling arithmetic is 15% of ARR at the worst 3.0% rate, or 0.45 points of gross margin; at realistic rates and assuming only part of channel-influenced ARR transacts on a marketplace, the drag is 0.1-0.3 points. Non-GAAP gross margin declined 380 basis points from its Q4 2023 peak of 83.4% to 79.6% in Q2 2026. The channel explains at most one eighth of that.▪

First-half 2026 cost of revenue, by line:

Line 1H 2025 1H 2026 Change
Revenue $1,588.3m $2,127.9m +34.0%
Cost of revenue $323.6m $449.3m +38.9%
GAAP gross margin 79.63% 78.88% (75)bp
Third-party cloud hosting and software [estimate] ~$248m, 15.6% of revenue ~$354m, 16.6% of revenue +100bp of revenue
Personnel and other cost of revenue ~$76m, 4.8% of revenue ~$95m, 4.5% of revenue (30)bp of revenue

The hosting line accounts for the whole of the decline and slightly more, and personnel offsets part of it. Nothing is left for marketplace fees or product mix.

Amazon's own filing points the other way on price. Amazon's FY2025 10-K states that AWS sales growth was "partially offset by pricing changes primarily driven by long-term customer contracts", which is price conceded down to large committed buyers. Datadog's CEO said on the Q3 2024 call that "we also keep getting better and better agreements with our cloud providers as we scale." Both layers are absorbing the same AI-era infrastructure cost inflation at once: Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud gross margin declined 420 basis points in the window Datadog's declined 180, explicitly "driven by the continued investments in AI infrastructure", and AWS's operating margin declined from 37.0% to 35.4%. If the hyperscalers had gained pricing power over Datadog their own margins would be expanding.▪

The disclosed candidates for why hosting per revenue dollar rose are in management's own words:

  • AI-native workloads at scale: "our cloud hosting costs rose more quickly than we expected in Q1, as we supported large growth spikes from some of our largest customers" (Q1 2025).
  • New features shipped before optimisation: "we build new features… will have more compute impact and more storage impact… Maybe also they won't be fantastically optimised on day one" (Q2 2024).
  • A deliberate reallocation of engineering effort: "when gross margins get a little bit low, we put more effort on optimising" (Q3 2024).

Against that, asked on the Q4 2025 call whether large AI-native customers are dilutive to gross margin, the CFO answered "On a weighted average, they're not… it isn't about the AI-natives or non-AI-natives, it has to do with the size of the customer." That answer addresses discount structure, not cost to serve, and the two answers conflict.

5.3 The binding constraint is downstream

Test Evidence Result
Has capacity ever limited revenue? The 10-K risk factor is conditional: "Any limitation on the capacity of our third-party hosting services could impede our ability to onboard new customers." No 10-K or 10-Q in seven years reports an actual capacity-driven shortfall Not binding
Is Datadog capital-constrained in adding capacity? Capex plus capitalised software was $135.4m in FY2025, 4.0% of revenue, against $5.0bn of cash and securities at 2026-06-30 Not binding
Does Datadog own physical capacity it must fill? Item 2 Properties lists only ~395,000 sq ft of leased New York office space. "We outsource substantially all of the infrastructure relating to our cloud solution to third-party hosting services" No fixed-cost capacity risk
Is demand concentrated enough to move guidance? Q3 2026 guided to $1,135-1,145m, +1.7% sequentially at the midpoint against +7.6%, +5.6% and +11.4% in the prior three quarters, because of one customer's usage reduction Binding

Datadog's realized price per unit of monitored infrastructure is set against a free open-source alternative at the customer.

The purchase commitments are a rate agreement. Non-cancelable purchase commitments, "primarily related to cloud hosting and other software-based services" and "due primarily over the next 5 years":

At 31 Dec Purchase commitments Operating leases Est. annual hosting cost [estimate] Commitments ÷ annual hosting
2021 $688.4m $97.0m ~$192m 3.6x
2022 $721.5m $326.6m ~$274m 2.6x
2023 $485.0m $347.1m ~$311m 1.6x
2024 $1,400m $365.6m ~$390m 3.6x
2025 $1,400m $375.2m ~$390-540m 2.6-3.6x

The commitment is written to roughly 3.5x the then-current annual hosting run-rate and allowed to amortise toward 1.5x before renewal. The 2024 renewal roughly tripled the dollar commitment while the run-rate rose about 25%, which is how volume buys a rate; management said as much in the quarter it would have been negotiated.▪ Spread over five years, $1.4bn is about $280m a year against $380-550m of annual hosting, so the commitment covers roughly half to three-quarters of actual consumption and revenue would have to decline substantially before Datadog paid for capacity it did not use. Neither side is locked in: $1.4bn is 0.57% of the $244bn of long-term AWS customer commitments Amazon disclosed at December 2025, and a smaller fraction of Microsoft's $678bn commercial remaining performance obligation. Datadog's spend is immaterial to any one hyperscaler, and on Datadog's side $1.4bn against $5.0bn of liquidity is not coercive either.

Bring-your-own-cloud shifts cost off Datadog's books and lowers the price it charges. BYOC shifts storage and retrieval cost from Datadog's cost of revenue to the customer's own cloud account, raising Datadog's gross margin on those workloads and lowering the effective price the customer pays Datadog. It reduces Datadog's hosting bill without reducing the hyperscalers' total take from the chain.▪ No sizing is disclosed. The 10-K states Datadog outsources substantially all infrastructure and Item 2 lists no datacenter real estate, so the UK "data center" announced in Q1 2026 is a Datadog region on third-party infrastructure.

5.4 Customer-side economics

Infrastructure Pro plus APM at list is $46 per host per month, against a general-purpose mid-size cloud instance costing roughly $50-150 a month on demand. At list, monitoring a host with two Datadog products is of the same order as running it. Volume discounts at enterprise scale reduce that, but the list-price ratio is why cost-driven churn to open source is the standing failure mode and why Flex Logs and Logging Without Limits exist.

At the market level, observability is a low-single-digit percentage of all cloud services spend and a high-single-digit to low-teens percentage of the cloud infrastructure spend it monitors. Gartner's $28bn observability figure for 2026E against roughly $890bn of public cloud services is about 3.1%; against the infrastructure-and-platform portion, roughly half the total, about 6%; practitioner benchmarks put it at 7-15% of cloud infrastructure spend and higher for Kubernetes-heavy estates [web, low source quality, directional only].

Datadog's own penetration statistic is a median:

Metric Value Date
Fortune 500 logo penetration 48% are customers Dec-2025
Median Datadog spend per Fortune 500 customer less than $0.5m (disclosed only as a bound) Dec-2025
Global account opportunities >470,000 Dec-2025
Datadog logo penetration of that universe 7% Dec-2025
Channel-influenced ARR 15% of total Dec-2025

Source: [deck: Investor Day 2026, 2026-02-12, slides 131, 137, 177]. Half the Fortune 500 have a Datadog account and the typical one spends less than a single senior engineer costs, so Datadog has a departmental foothold in most of the Fortune 500.▪ The expansion runway inside existing logos is arithmetically larger than the new-logo runway, and the cohort multiples support it: the 2019 cohort had grown to 9.7x its first-year ARR by 2025, the 2020 cohort 3.9x and the 2021 cohort 2.3x [deck: Investor Day 2026, 2026-02-12, slide 164]. The same cohorts were restated upward between the 2024 and 2026 decks, most sharply the 2019 vintage, from 4.4x to 9.7x, with nothing on the slide flagging it, and 2019 is the vintage in which the large AI-native accounts landed.

The addressable account universe also shrank between the two decks, from more than 530,000 (February 2024) to more than 470,000 (February 2026), with no explanation, so the improvement in stated logo penetration from 5% to 7% is partly a smaller denominator.

The customer's return is asserted. Datadog's case in the deck is illustrative: incident resolution compressing from "hours or days" with "hundreds of engineers called" to "under one hour" and "dozens of engineers", and with Bits AI agents to "minutes" and "under 10 engineers". All three slides are labelled "Illustrative Example", and every customer ROI figure in the deck set is labelled "based on information provided by the customer and Datadog internal analysis". Those are customer self-reports. That matters for durability: a customer paying under $0.5m a year needs only a modest number of avoided incident-hours to justify it, and the arithmetic is easy at that size. A customer paying nine figures is buying at a scale where the case has to be made on the cost of the alternative build. That is the customer whose usage reduced in Q3 2026.

5.5 Bargaining-power trajectory

Hyperscaler to Datadog: power has not shifted. Quarterly non-GAAP gross margin from the calls runs 83.4% (Q4 2023), 83.3%, 82.1%, 81.1%, 81.7%, 80.3%, 80.9%, 81.2%, 81.4% (Q4 2025), 80.2%, 79.6% (Q2 2026) — six declines and four increases across ten quarters, a 380-basis-point net decline from the peak, and the first sub-80% print since Q1 2022. Against that, Datadog's unit rate is improving by management's account, its spend is immaterial to any one supplier, it owns no capacity that would strand on a switch, and the hyperscalers' own margins are compressing on the same AI infrastructure cost. Both layers are absorbing the same input inflation.

Datadog to customer: power is increasing across the mass of the base and decreasing at the very top. Net retention improved from high-110%'s (Dec-2024) to about 120% (Dec-2025) to low-120%'s (Jun-2026). Gross retention was stable at mid-to-high 90s. Multi-product adoption improved on every threshold. The structural headwind is per-host pricing against instances that keep getting larger — Pomel, Q1 2022: "the type of hosts that our customers buy also is changing over time, that they're also getting larger and larger instances from the cloud providers that costs more and more." A fixed dollar per host on a growing host is a declining share of the customer's compute dollar, which is why attach is necessary.▪ The largest accounts are the exception: one big enough to build its own observability cut usage.

Remaining performance obligations stalled. Remaining performance obligations went $3,461.2m (2025-12-31) → $3,484.4m (2026-03-31) → $3,471.4m (2026-06-30), which is +0.3% across two quarters after +42.7% over the prior two, and the second of those quarters contained a disclosed nine-figure renewal and a disclosed multi-year deal of over $30m of total contract value. Year-over-year RPO is still +43% and current RPO about +40%, and billings grew 38% in Q2 2026, faster than revenue, so collections are not the issue. Either the renewal was executed after 30 June or it replaced a larger prior commitment. The two are not reconciled.

6. Secular and industry trends

6.1 The 2025-26 acceleration is not the AI-native cohort

Datadog discloses the cohort's contribution to year-over-year revenue growth in each filing, and the series is flat while total growth accelerated seven points:

Quarter Total revenue growth AI-native contribution (filed) Non-AI-native growth (management, on call)
Q2 2025 28.1% ~10 pts 18%
Q3 2025 28.4% approximately 8 pts 20%
Q4 2025 29.2% approximately 7 pts 23%
Q1 2026 32.2% high single digits mid-20s
Q2 2026 35.6% high single digit pts high 20s

Each row sums: 20+8 = 28, 23+7 = 30 against 29 reported, 25+8 = 33 against 32, 28+8 = 36 against 36. Total growth rose 7.2 points between Q3 2025 and Q2 2026 while the AI-native contribution went from about 8 points to about 8 points. Every point of the acceleration came from the non-AI-native base.

The corollary matters as much. A cohort contributing a flat number of growth points while the company grows 30%+ is a cohort whose own growth rate is compressing hard.▪ Cohort revenue was roughly $91m in Q2 2025 (11% of $826.8m, disclosed) and roughly $157m in Q2 2026, so cohort growth ran about +70% against roughly +250% in the year to Q2 2025. [estimate: the disclosed 11% share rolled forward at the disclosed 8-point growth contribution; across a 7-10 point contribution assumption the cohort is $149-174m per quarter, 13.3-15.5% of revenue, growing +64% to +91%]. That deceleration is what management warned of in Q3 2024: "some of the large customers in this cohort have ramped extremely rapidly and … may optimize cloud and observability usage."

The Q2 2026 call added hyperscaler in-house AI labs to the cohort and did not say whether prior periods were restated, so the five-quarter non-AI acceleration series may not be on a constant basis. The cohort "now also includes hyperscalers using Datadog for in-house AI labs." Reclassifying customers between the AI and non-AI buckets changes both disclosed growth rates.

The implied share column reproduces Datadog's own separately published market-share chart to within 0.1 point in all six years, which is what validates the chart reading.]

Decomposing 2020 to 2026E: Datadog's revenue rose 7.39x (39.6% compound), the market rose about 2.1x (roughly 13% compound), and share rose 3.56x from 4.5% to 15.9%. The identity checks: 2.07 × 3.56 = 7.37 against 7.39. In log terms 64% of Datadog's growth came from taking share and 36% from the market expanding, and the market excluding Datadog compounded at 10.5% while Datadog compounded at 39.6%, 3.8x the rest of its own market. The end market does not grow at anything close to Datadog's rate, so every year of 25-30% growth requires another two to three points of share from a base already near 16%.▪

Against the pure-play peer cohort, Datadog outgrew the two closest listed comparables by roughly 17 points a year for five straight years: five-year calendar CAGRs of 41.5% against Dynatrace's 24.1% and Elastic's 24.8%.▪ Its share of the three-vendor pool went from 26.8% (mid-2019) to 35.9% (mid-2021) to 50.8% (mid-2026), a monotone 24-point gain in seven years, while the pool itself compounded 29.6% and Datadog compounded 39.0% over the last five. Search is the majority of Elastic's revenue and observability the minority, and Dynatrace had a perpetual-to-subscription conversion tail through FY2021; both caveats belong.

Against the ultimate volume driver, the decisive check runs the other way.

Period AWS sales growth DDOG revenue growth
FY2025 +20% +27.7%
Q1 2026 +28% +32.2%
Q2 2026 +37% +35.6%

Datadog grew slower than AWS in Q2 2026, which has not happened at any point in the company's public life. The ultimate driver accelerated 17 points from FY2025 to Q2 2026; Datadog accelerated 7.9 points.▪

6.3 The one observable downcycle

Datadog has exactly one downcycle on the tape, the 2022-23 cloud-optimisation episode, and it is the only empirical estimate of amplitude available.

  • Revenue growth: 82.8% (Q1 2022) to 25.4% (Q2 2023), a 57-point deceleration over five quarters.
  • Sequential revenue add: +$43.1m (Q2 2022) to +$12.3m (Q1 2023), a 71% decline in dollar adds, with sequential growth troughing at +2.6%.
  • Growth never went negative and sequential adds never went negative. The trough was a plateau at 25-27% for six consecutive quarters.
  • Net retention: above 130% (2021, the disclosed band) to mid-110%'s (2023) to about 120% (2025) to low-120%'s (Q2 2026). Gross retention never moved through any of it, so the entire 15-point net-retention swing came from expansion.

Beta to the driver: AWS growth over the same window went from 37% (Q1 2022) to 12% (Q2 2023), a 25-point deceleration, against Datadog's 57 points: Datadog's growth declined roughly 2.3 points for each point AWS declined. In the current upswing, measured on the same FY2025-to-Q2-2026 window, AWS has added 17 points and Datadog 7.9, so Datadog is rising about 0.5 points per point of AWS acceleration. On a proportional measure the asymmetry survives at roughly 1.9x down and 0.4x up. That asymmetry is the most important thing the episode teaches and management commentary does not address it. If AWS decelerates from +37% back toward its 2025 rate of +20%, a 17-point move, the historical downside beta implies Datadog retracing far more than the 7.9 points it has gained. Neither Bloomberg consensus nor the driver-based model in Section 17 links Datadog's growth to hyperscaler growth.

Management identified the turn roughly two quarters after the trough in the numbers and called the end six quarters after the start, declining to call a bottom throughout: "visibility remains limited as to when this optimization cycle will end, but we firmly believe it will" (Q1 2023). Recovery to the prior growth rate never happened. Datadog exited the episode at 25-27%, and stripping the AI-native cohort out, the pre-2022 base grows in the high 20s today against the 60-80% that preceded the downcycle. Management frames optimisation as a cycle that passed, which is accurate about the rate of change and silent about the level.

6.4 Penetration against wallet

As of Fortune 500 penetration Median Fortune 500 ARR
Jan 2022 30% —
Jan 2023 37% "in the hundreds of thousands of dollars"
Dec 2023 42% "still less than $0.5 million"
Dec 2024 45% "still less than $0.5 million"
Dec 2025 48% "still less than $0.5 million"

Logo penetration advanced 18 points in four years while the median wallet stayed inside the same disclosed band for four consecutive years. Management has said explicitly where it expects that to go — "customer on the Fortune 500, that's in the hundreds of thousands should be in the millions to tens of millions with us in the end" (Q4 2023 call) — and four years of disclosure show it has not moved out of the band. Expansion is concentrated. Customers at $1m+ went 216 (2021) → 317 → 396 → 462 → 603 (2025), with growth re-accelerating from +17% to +31%, and customers at $100k+ reached 4,720 at Q2 2026, +23% year over year and accelerating for six straight quarters. Those customers are 91% of ARR.

Net customer adds are falling. Sequential net customer adds ran +800, +500, +900, +600, +700, +500 and +200 across the seven quarters to Q2 2026, and year-over-year customer growth went from +9.9% (Q4 2024) to +6.4% (Q2 2026). The +200 is the smallest in at least ten quarters and it happened in a DASH user-conference quarter that added 900 a year earlier, which an Oppenheimer analyst put directly to management as "probably the weakest quarter I ever remember." Management's answer is that gross additions are on trend and the variability sits "at the very low end, the border between free and contract" with "very little effect on revenues", and the same quarter's new-logo annualized bookings more than doubled with new customers supplying 30% of year-over-year revenue growth against 25% in Q1. Both are disclosed and one quarter does not settle it. Counts are rounded to the nearest hundred, so ±100 of noise sits on the +200.

Geography narrowed too. Revenue from outside North America was 27% of 1H 2026 revenue against 29% in 1H 2025. On the disclosed dollars in Note 11, North America grew from $1,120.5m to $1,548.6m (+38.2%) while International grew from $467.8m to $579.3m (+23.8%), a 14.4-point gap. Management attributes it to where the AI activity is: "We see particular strength in the Americas as much of the AI activity is occurring in the U.S." (Q2 2026 call). International share peaked at 30.2% in FY2024, and FY2025 was the first year since FY2019 in which North America outgrew International. International revenue was $994m in FY2025, larger than the entire Log Management pillar, and it is decelerating while North America is not.

6.5 Multi-product attach is the durable mechanism, and it is working in the deep tail

Year-over-year point gains in the 6+ product bucket were +4 (2023), +4 (2024), +7 (2025) and +8 (Q2 2026 against Q2 2025); in the 8+ bucket +3, +3, +6, +8; in the 10+ bucket +3 (2025) and +6 (Q2 2026 against Q2 2025). Existing customers supplied 70-75% of the revenue increase in every disclosed period from FY2021 through 1H 2026, with Q2 2026's shift to 70% existing and 30% new the first move toward new customers in three years.

The deck adds the qualification the calls do not. Added ARR by type ran roughly 26% new customers, 57% expansion of existing products and 17% cross-sell of new products in 2025, against 44%, 37% and 19% in 2023▪ [deck: Investor Day 2026, 2026-02-12, slide 166]. Cross-sell of new products has been flat in an 11-21% band for six years while the product count went from 9 to 25. Growth is consumption expansion inside existing products far more than it is multi-product land-grab, and 2025 was the least new-logo-driven year on record.

6.6 Technology shifts that could change the slope

OpenTelemetry is neutralised for now. The disclosed metric that would show a slope change first is the 6+/8+/10+ attach series stalling, because correlation across products is what OpenTelemetry does not commoditise.

Open-source cost repatriation — traffic runs both ways. Pomel's economic argument is the strongest thing in the bull case and it is checkable: "for any dollars customers spend on us, they're going to spend $10 or $20 on their cloud provider. They're going to spend $20 to $100 on their engineering team" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). At $4.46bn of FY2026 guided revenue the implied cloud spend of Datadog's customer base is $45-90bn, plausible against combined hyperscaler scale, which makes the spend-ratio claim credible. It also contains its own counterweight, which Pomel states: if the "$20 to $100 on their engineering team" migrates to AI models, "maybe some of that … is actually going to go to these AI models instead." AI is attacking the same engineering budget that makes Datadog's bill look small.

AI coding agents — the surface-area evidence. The bear case was put to management directly by Morgan Stanley: "observability is just data ingestion into a time series database … the implication is that observability can be replicated with the help of AI and coding agents." The evidence that agents increase surface area is real and entirely usage-based: MCP tool calls 11x, then 4x, then 4x across three quarters; LLM spans 10x over six months; Bits Assistant messages 12x quarter over quarter in Q1 2026. Management's stated reason is that with code "largely written by AI agents… you also need to spend a lot more time understanding how that code is working and that largely happens in production" (Q2 2025). And Datadog is not seat-priced: its units are hosts, containers, GPUs, sessions, tests and log volume, all of which scale with workload, not with developer headcount, so the "AI shrinks engineering teams" thesis does not touch its pricing unit directly.▪ What tempers it: none of the MCP or Bits AI metrics has revenue attached, and the only sizing available places every AI product inside the eighteen below $50m of ARR.

Regulatory and sovereignty shifts are additive and slow. FedRAMP High arrived in Q1 2026, a UK datacenter was announced in the same quarter, and cloud-prem deployment extended to logs at DASH 2026. Each unlocks a bounded, previously inaccessible workload pool over a multi-year timeline, and sovereignty requirements also raise Datadog's own cost to serve, because regional capacity is fixed cost against a model built for the opposite.

6.7 What would show first if the secular story were breaking

  1. Multi-product attach in the 6+/8+/10+ buckets stalls. A year-over-year point gain falling back to +3-4 from the current +7-8 is the cleanest early signal, and it is disclosed quarterly on the call.
  2. The $100k+ cohort's growth decelerates. +23% at Q2 2026 after six quarters of acceleration, and 91% of ARR comes from it. Quarterly, in the press release.
  3. AI-native contribution prints below the 7-9 point band, or reverts to a purely qualitative description. Quarterly, in Item 1A.
  4. Non-AI-native growth stops accelerating. Five straight quarters to high-20s. Call commentary only.
  5. Trailing gross revenue retention slips out of the mid-to-high 90s. Call commentary only, never filed, and the metric that would show OpenTelemetry-enabled churn first.
  6. Hyperscaler consumption growth rolls over. Reported roughly a week before Datadog, at a historical downside beta near 2x, this is the earliest available warning.
  7. Total customer count sequential adds stay at 200-300 for two more quarters while $100k+ growth also rolls over, which would mean the land motion is broken.
  8. International revenue share keeps declining. From 29% to 27% in twelve months; at 25% the geographic diversification argument is finished.

7. Critical points

1. One 10-Q reports 36% growth and the largest customer cutting usage. Q2 2026 revenue of $1,121.5m grew 36% year over year with a record $115m sequential addition, the FY2026 guide was raised $140m to $4.45-4.47bn, and the same 10-Q disclosed that the largest customer reduced usage beginning in Q3 2026. The Q3 guide implies +1.7% sequential growth against a four-year Q2-to-Q3 norm of +6.9% to +7.5%. On the guide grossed up by Datadog's historical mean beat, the implied reduction is $11-18m a quarter; on a counterfactual matching Q2's exceptional sequential, roughly $60m a quarter. The customer renewed on a nine-figure contract using 17 products.

2. Growth has moved almost entirely to spend per customer while the account base has stopped growing. Customers grew 6.4% year over year at Q2 2026 against 35.6% revenue growth, and net adds were +200 in a DASH quarter that added 900 a year earlier. Meanwhile customers at $100k+ grew 23%, customers at $1m+ grew 31% in 2025, and the 10+ product tier went from 5% to 13% of customers in eighteen months. Every disclosed expansion metric is accelerating and the land metric is not, so the growth base is narrowing at the same time it is deepening.

3. Gross margin is where the competitive structure shows up, and it is compressing while volume grows. Non-GAAP gross margin declined 380 basis points from 83.4% (Q4 2023) to 79.6% (Q2 2026), the first sub-80% print since Q1 2022, with $64.1m of the $74.1m Q2 2026 cost-of-revenue increase attributed to third-party cloud hosting. At FY2026 guided revenue, 380 basis points is roughly $169m of gross profit, about 17% of the $1.01-1.03bn non-GAAP operating income guide. The counterparties setting that cost also sell competing native monitoring and take marketplace margin on Datadog's own sales.

4. The whole of operating profit is the stock-compensation add-back, and that gap is closing slowly. FY2025 non-GAAP operating income of $768.0m sat against a GAAP operating loss of $44.4m, an $812m difference. GAAP net income of $107.7m existed only because of $171.4m of other income, almost all interest on the securities portfolio. The one favourable break in the recent record is that stock compensation declined to 19.6% of revenue in Q2 2026 from 21.8% a year earlier, the first sustained leverage in the company's history. It comes from revenue accelerating: dollar grant value was roughly flat year over year while revenue grew 34%.

5. Realized price is flat by management's own arithmetic, and deliberately deflating at the top. Blended price holds only because new small customers enter at list while the largest accounts receive volume discounts. Datadog also engineers price down as product strategy: one enterprise customer's indexed-log volume rose about 75x while unit price declined to roughly 5% of its 2021 level, producing about 4x the revenue. Revenue growth here requires volume to outrun price deflation, which works while volume grows and inverts when it does not.

6. Two-thirds of the growth has been share gain from a market that grows at 13%. Datadog's revenue rose 7.39x from 2020 to 2026E while the observability market it points to rose 2.07x, so 64% of the growth was share and 36% was the market. The market excluding Datadog compounded at 10.5%. Every additional year at 25-30% requires two to three more points of share from a base near 16%. And in Q2 2026 Datadog grew slower than AWS for the first time in its public life. Its growth fell roughly 2.3 points per point of AWS deceleration in the last downcycle and has risen about 0.5 points per point on the way up.

7. The AI exposure is much wider than the AI-native cohort. The cohort was 11% of revenue in 2025 and supplied roughly a third of the FY2025 revenue increase. But the share of ARR held by customers running one or more AI integrations went from ~45% (2023) to ~62% (2024) to ~72% (2025) [deck: Investor Day 2026, 2026-02-12, slide 174]. The 86-89% of revenue described as insulating is not insulated if the AI capital-expenditure cycle turns; the concentrated risk and the correlated risk are different sizes and the second is far larger.

8. Concentration is deeper than the filings show, and the deck shows it. No customer has ever been disclosed at 10% of revenue, but 34 customers held more than $10m of ARR at Dec-2025 — at least $340m, more than 8% of ARR from 0.1% of accounts — and 603 customers at $1m+ hold an estimated 56-66% of total ARR. The $10m+ tier appears in no 10-K.

9. Capital allocation has one variable and it is dilution. Eighty-two cents of every dollar Datadog has generated or raised since the IPO is still on the balance sheet, at $4,985m of cash and securities at 2026-06-30. There has never been a buyback or a dividend, so gross issuance equals net dilution. Shares outstanding compounded 2.95% a year over six and a half years, at or above the top of management's own 2.5-3.0% target in each of the last three years, and 62.6m shares issued since 2019 were worth $7,188m at the respective years' average prices against $3,542m of cumulative free cash flow.

10. The advantage is real, earns above its cost of capital, and is not widening. On an R&D-capitalized basis Datadog earns 17.1% on invested capital against a 9-11% cost of capital. The stock-comp-excluded operating margin moved 2.4 points while revenue doubled, and both the gross-margin and operating-margin gaps against Dynatrace re-widened after 2023. Datadog is winning volume and losing the returns-per-dollar comparison, which is the correct trade if the market is unpenetrated.

8. Management claim pressure tests

The AI-native disclosure improved as the exposure grew. Management published the cohort's revenue share for six quarters, peaking at 12% in Q3 2025, pre-announced its retirement in the same sentence as the last disclosure, and has not published it since; asked directly on the Q4 2025 call, Obstler answered "We didn't — have not put it in there." What survives is a percentage-point contribution to growth, disclosed in the risk factor of the 10-K and 10-Q instead of on the call, plus cohort head counts that only rise. The asymmetry is arithmetic: a growth-contribution figure rises with the cohort while the revenue base at risk goes unstated. On Q2 2026 revenue of $1,121.5m against a $826.8m prior-year base, 8 points of growth is about $66m of the $294.7m year-over-year increase, 22% of all incremental revenue, from a cohort whose revenue share is no longer published. Two facts qualify the charge and are stated with it: the share was disclosed for six quarters, and the deck published the full-year series (1%, 1%, 2%, 5%, 11% of revenue for 2021-2025) four months after the calls stopped.

"Our guidance conservatism is intact, so the Q3 guide is another sandbag." Datadog has beaten its quarterly revenue guide 27 times in 27 quarters, and the last eight beats ranged 3.1-5.2%, mean 4.25%. Three convergent methods put FY2026 at $4.59-4.62bn if nothing had changed, against a guide midpoint of $4.46bn, so the implied cushion is 3.0-3.6% against a historical Q2-vintage median of 3.49%. The cushion is the same size; what changed is what it is reserved against. For the first time in the post-IPO record the cushion is reserved against a negative that has already occurred and been disclosed. On that arithmetic the largest customer's reduction is roughly the size of one year's usual conservatism, about $130-160m of full-year revenue, and if it is worth more than about $150m the guide has no cushion left at all. The guided sequential of +1.7% is also the weakest in four years against a guided average of +2.3% and a realized average of +7.2%.

"Management guides conservatively on profit as well as revenue." The revenue record supports it; the profit record no longer does to the same degree. The non-GAAP operating income beat against midpoint compressed from a median of 27.3% across all 25 guided quarters to 10.2% across the last eight, and to $2.5m or 1.5% in Q1 2025. Datadog now converts almost none of the revenue upside into a profit beat, by design: "we've tended to have some of that flow through into the margin line and then re-up again for the next phase of growth" (Q4 2025). Applying the all-history median beat to the Q3 2026 guide midpoint of $265m gives $337m; applying the trailing-eight mean gives $292m. The gap is $45m in one quarter.

"The 25%+ long-term operating margin target is a floor the company is walking back toward." The trajectory runs the other way. The non-GAAP operating margin was 25% in 2024, 22% in 2025, and the FY2026 guide implies 22.9%, a second consecutive year at or below 23%. The target has been reaffirmed twice without a date and without a path, while the underlying spend targets moved up: the IPO-era research goal of 22-26% of revenue is now described as "around 30%".▪ R&D at 30% of the FY2026 guide midpoint is $1,338m against $1,160m at the old goal's upper bound, and that $178m difference is 4.0 points of operating margin, which accounts for the whole gap between the 22.9% guided and the 25%+ goal. Management's stated line-item targets (R&D ~30%, S&M mid-20s, G&A ~5%) sum to about 60% of revenue, which against an 80% gross margin caps the non-GAAP operating margin near 20%, below what the company is currently guiding.▪ Both sets of numbers were given at the same investor day and neither document reconciles them.

"Gross margin runs at 80% plus or minus, and there is no change in our expectations." Obstler said that on the Q2 2026 call, attributing variation to "investments into innovations for our customers, offset by efficiency efforts." The 10-Q filed days later attributes the decline "primarily as a result of increased spend with our third-party cloud infrastructure provider costs", with $64.1m of the $74.1m quarterly increase named. Investment offset by efficiency and hyperscaler cost inflation are different explanations with different durability, and the realized series has declined in six of the ten quarters since the Q4 2023 peak, reaching the lowest print since Q1 2022.

"About 3x the R&D spend of our next closest peer." Exactly right against the pure-plays, at 3.3x Dynatrace and 3.4x Elastic on GAAP research expense, and 3.0x and 3.2x on a like-for-like non-GAAP basis. Exactly wrong against the platform competitors named in Datadog's own competition section, who outspend it by 5-23x in total research even though only a fraction goes to observability. The claim's validity depends entirely on the definition of "our market", which management does not state.

"Penetration is 7% of a curated 470,000-account target market." Set against year-over-year customer growth of 6.4% at 2026-06-30, either the target market overstates the reachable universe or the low-end motion has lost effectiveness. The deck supplies a partial answer that management did not: the addressable account universe was restated downward from more than 530,000 (February 2024) to more than 470,000 (February 2026) with no explanation, so the stated improvement from 5% to 7% penetration is partly a smaller denominator.

"We have been very disciplined and gotten very high returns from our acquisition strategy." Three of twenty post-IPO deals produced nothing that survives: CoScreen was shut down on 2026-07-31 and still appears on the platform slide of the investor presentation dated 2026-08-06. Seekret has no named product. Actiondesk was mentioned once. None of that is visible anywhere in the accounts, and it cannot be: $696m of post-IPO goodwill additions show zero impairment in every year from 2018 through mid-2026, because a single reporting unit whose fair value is the whole company cannot fail a test on a $40m tuck-in. The clean impairment record is a property of the structure.

"Datadog's M&A is small and immaterial." True of the seven-year total and no longer true of the run-rate. First-half 2026 booked $191.5m of consideration and $178.7m of goodwill in six months, against $178.4m and $163.1m for all of FY2025 and $70.3m of goodwill across 2022-2024 combined. Goodwill grew 33.2% in six months, and roughly half of all post-IPO consideration has been committed since 1 January 2025.

"Our job is not to accumulate on the balance sheet." The CFO said that at a Barclays conference on 2023-12-06, adding "now is not the right time, but we do look at that." Cash and securities went from $2,583m at that date to $4,985m at 2026-06-30, +93%. In 2023 Datadog traded below $100 on 190 of 250 trading days with a low of $62.69, holding cash equal to 12.5% of its own market capitalisation. The honest counter-argument is that a buyback large enough to offset dilution was not affordable out of free cash flow in any year on record — the cost was $1,068m (FY2023), $1,382m and $1,389m against free cash flow of $598m, $775m and $915m — so the shortfall was $470-607m a year and would be roughly $1.5bn at today's price.

"Our long-term revenue growth is not something we will target." Datadog has never issued a long-term revenue target and gives a consistent reason: "we are built on digital transformation and cloud migration. And we don't fully control that groundswell or the rate of migration of that groundswell." The only standing long-term financial commitment is a single undated margin number, and the disclosure that set the growth expectation — 130%+ net retention sustained over 16 quarters, published in the 2021 deck — is gone, replaced by a band.▪

Leadership: The founder layer is unchanged in sixteen years: Pomel as CEO since founding, Lê-Quôc as CTO and, since December 2024, President. David Obstler has been CFO since November 2018. The layer beneath has turned over roughly every three to four years — Amit Agarwal left in December 2024 after twelve years as Chief Product Officer and then President, joining ICONIQ Capital and returning to the Datadog board the following month; Yanbing Li took the product role from outside in August 2024; the go-to-market seat has changed hands at least three times. No named executive officer has departed in a way requiring a severance disclosure in any of the eight proxies.

What never happened: No workforce reduction, no restructuring charge, no goodwill impairment and no share repurchase appears anywhere in the seven 10-Ks, in a company that lived through 2022-23.

The four inflections that changed the trajectory

  • The 2020 COVID shock was a false inflection, and it is the control experiment. Growth decelerated 31 points in three quarters and then returned to 84%. Net retention never left the "over 130%" band for a single quarter. $100k+ net adds dipped to 55 in Q2 2020 and were back to 184 by Q1 2021. That is what a shock to Datadog's demand looks like when the underlying workload does not change. The 2022-23 episode is what it looks like when it does, and in that one net retention lost 15 points and has never recovered them.
  • The 2022-23 optimisation downcycle changed the business, and management chose its response. Headcount growth went from 50% (2022) to 8% (2023) with no layoffs, no restructuring charge, and the recruiting organisation deliberately preserved: "last year, when the market was slowing down, most of our peers have laid off their recruiting teams, and we didn't do that because we knew we need to — our success will depend on revving the recruiting engine back up." Non-GAAP operating margin rose through the trough, from 19.5% (FY2022) to 23.0% (FY2023), and free cash flow margin from 21.1% to 28.1%. That choice was available because the company held roughly $1.7bn of cash and generated $353.5m of free cash flow with no operational need for capital. Expect the same shape next time: margin widening during the downturn and reversing when growth returns.
  • Platform breadth saturated in 2023 and the mechanism switched to depth. The 2+ product metric — 25% of customers at end-2018, 72% at Q4 2020, 83% at Q4 2023 — has added two points in three years, and from Q1 2026 the prepared remarks lead with the 4+ figure instead, with no quarter announcing the change. Over the same period the 4+ band went 42% → 58%, the 6+ band 18% → 37% and the 10+ band from nothing to 13%. The number of customers is no longer the growth variable; spend per customer is, and that is the same variable that collapsed in 2022-23.
  • The AI-native cohort, 2023 to now, and its Q3 2026 reversal. First named on the Q3 2023 call at about 2.5 points of growth, the cohort reached 11% of revenue in 2025 and supplied roughly a third of that year's revenue increase. The FY2024 10-K quantified it at ~5 points of Q4 2024 growth without saying the largest customer was inside it. The FY2025 10-K added that fact. The Q2 2026 10-Q disclosed the usage reduction. Revenue growth accelerated from 25% (Q1 2025) to 36% (Q2 2026), roughly 5-6 points of it from the cohort and roughly 5 points from the non-AI base, and the company is now guiding about 7 points of that back out in a single quarter because of one account. The cohort brought growth and brought gross-margin dilution with it.

Two candidates that did not qualify: The March 2023 outage was the worst possible reputational event for an observability vendor and is invisible in every KPI: gross retention stayed mid-to-high 90s through 2023, $100k+ customer adds in Q1 2023 were the best of that year, and the stock rose 14.5% on the print that disclosed it. Datadog took a reliability failure of the kind its product exists to prevent and suffered no commercial consequence in any KPI, which matters when underwriting the durability of the base. The security push is real and did not change any trajectory: five years after Sqreen, the suite crossed $100m of ARR in Q2 2025 — roughly 2.6% of ARR — growing mid-40s percent against a claimed $21bn cloud-security market.

What the current narrative reframes or omits

  • The level, not the rate, is what 2022-23 changed. The pre-2022 base grew 60-80%; the same base, stripped of AI-native customers, grows high-20s today. Management is accurate about the growth rate and silent about the level, and the ex-AI figures management now volunteers each quarter make it checkable.
  • The $1m+ ARR customer count decelerated a full year after revenue did. Growth in that cohort was +47% (2022), +25% (2023), +17% (2024) — the trough was 2024, a year after the revenue trough — before re-accelerating to +31% in 2025. It is disclosed once a year, in the 10-K.
  • The FY2020 $1m+ count was restated. The Q4 2020 release reported 97 and the Q4 2021 release reports the prior year as 101. Small, and a reminder that these operating metrics are unaudited and management-defined.
  • The Nevada redomiciliation is invisible in the investor narrative. It required a special stockholder meeting and a 383,000-character proxy and moved the company's governing law and exclusive forum. It appears in no earnings-call prepared remarks, and the next annual proxy contains a shareholder proposal for a simple-majority vote standard.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs it

Person Role Since
Olivier Pomel Co-founder, CEO, director 2010
Alexis Lê-Quôc Co-founder, President and CTO, director 2010 (President added after Dec 2024)
David Obstler CFO Nov 2018
Adam Blitzer COO May 2021
Sean Walters CRO Jan 2022 (SVP worldwide sales from 2018)
Yanbing Li Chief Product Officer Aug 2024
David Galloreese Chief People Officer Jul 2024
Kerry Acocella General Counsel Jan 2022

Eleven directors, in three staggered classes. Two seats are ICONIQ-affiliated and both waive all director compensation. Dev Ittycheria, CEO of MongoDB, has served since February 2014, holds 240,000 options — the largest option position on the board by a wide margin — and sits on the compensation committee while MongoDB is a member of the compensation peer group. No related-person transactions are disclosed for 2025 beyond indemnification agreements.

10.2 What the pay plan measures

Cash is small and static: base salaries of $450,000 for Pomel, Obstler, Lê-Quôc and Blitzer in 2025 with a target bonus of 94% of salary. Everything else is equity. Pomel's 2025 Summary Compensation Table total was $27.1m, of which $25.8m was stock awards; the CEO total moved $11.6m (2023) → $19.8m (2024) → $27.1m (2025), entirely on the equity line.

Instrument Metric Structure Outcome
Annual cash bonus Net new ARR, with decelerators if non-GAAP operating income falls below target Floor at 50%, cap at 200% 2025: ARR attainment 139%, operating-income target met, payout 183% of target
Long-term equity, 50% of grant Time-based RSUs Four-year service vest —
Long-term equity, 50% of grant PSUs on annual revenue, gated by a non-GAAP operating income target One-year performance period, four-year service vest, floor at 90% of the revenue target, cap at 200% 2023: 99.4% of target → 92% earned. 2024: 100.5% → 115%. 2025: 104.0% → 200%, capped

Fitting the three observed points, the payout curve moves roughly 21-24 points of payout per single point of revenue attainment, and caps at roughly 104% of target [estimate: linear interpolation of the three disclosed attainment-payout pairs from the 2024, 2025 and 2026 proxies]. A revenue beat of about 3.5% against plan therefore doubles the equity award, and for a usage-based business growing 25-30% a year, 3.5% of revenue is roughly six weeks of growth. The target is not soft: the FY2025 PSU target of $3,294m was 3.1% above the top of the revenue guidance management issued publicly on the Q4 2024 call. And the curve cuts both ways, as FY2023 missed and paid 92%. The 2026 proxy describes the goals as "challenging to attain" and says exceeding target "would, in the compensation committee's view, require extraordinary efforts", in the same paragraph as a 4.0% beat producing the capped payout.

What the plan does not measure: Neither instrument measures GAAP results, per-share results, free cash flow, dilution or relative total shareholder return. The single profitability condition in both is a threshold on non-GAAP operating income, which adds back the $750.7m of stock compensation that is the reason GAAP operating income is negative. Net share dilution is a stated capital-allocation target — 2.5-3.0% at the 2026 investor day, tightened from 2.5-3.5% in 2024 — and the compensation committee does not use it as a performance metric. Concretely, an executive earned 200% of target PSUs and 183% of target bonus in a year in which GAAP operating income was a $44.4m loss, GAAP net income of $107.7m existed only because of $171.4m of interest income, and the share count rose 3.0%.

Datadog has no stock ownership guidelines for executives or directors, across all eight proxies. For the founders that is immaterial; for the COO, who held 680 Class A shares at March 2026, and the CRO, who held 20,269, it is not. Severance is modest and double-trigger, with no excise-tax gross-ups, no single-trigger acceleration and no guaranteed bonuses, and there is a compliant clawback policy and a flat prohibition on hedging and pledging. Say-on-pay support has run 95-99% for five years.

Pay versus performance. FY2025 is the first year in the disclosed series in which cumulative Datadog total shareholder return is below the peer index (360 against 388), and it is also the year CEO compensation actually paid rose 70% to $50.1m. The two are not linked by the plan — compensation actually paid is a mark-to-market of unvested equity and the plan paid out on revenue. The plan's metrics track no external benchmark. The CEO pay ratio went from 45:1 for FY2021 to 131:1 for FY2025; over four years CEO Summary Compensation Table total rose 214% while median employee compensation rose 8.5%.

10.3 Voting control, the sunset, and the Nevada move

Class B has ten votes and Class A one. At 2026-06-30, 24,170,410 Class B shares represented approximately 42% of the voting power on roughly 6.8% of shares outstanding, a six-to-one gap between control and economics. The voting-power series decays about one point a year as Class B converts on transfer: 46% (2023-12-31), 44%, 43%, 43% (2026-03-31), 42% (2026-06-30). Insider voting power at each proxy record date went 42.6% (2020) → 55.8% (2022) → 40.5% (2025) → 35.5% (2026), so the bloc held an outright majority from 2021 through 2023 and lost it during 2024. At 35.5% it retains a blocking position on everything requiring two thirds, which includes any stockholder amendment to the bylaws and amendments to the charter articles governing board composition, written consent, exculpation and forum.

The sunset is about September 2029 and the redomiciliation did not reset it. The Nevada articles adopted in April 2026 define the Final Conversion Date as the tenth anniversary of the effective time of the pre-IPO Delaware charter, and Class A first traded on 2019-09-19. On that date every Class B share converts and no further Class B may be issued. The sunset clock runs from the 2019 charter, not the 2026 conversion. A reset would have pushed it to 2036.

The Nevada conversion, completed 2026-04-21. The board's first stated reason, and the only one specific to Datadog, is founder flexibility: "Nevada Law Will Preserve Necessary Flexibility for Our Founders' Involvement… preserving our flexibility to keep Mr. Pomel and Mr. Lê-Quôc involved in running the Company". The same section adds that "the statute-driven approach adopted by Nevada … would offer our founders, Board and management clearer guideposts for considering and making changes to those arrangements in the future if deemed desirable and appropriate." What changes in substance: Nevada codifies the business judgment rule and, per the proxy's own comparison, its Supreme Court has applied it to transactions that would face entire-fairness review in Delaware; the 2025 amendments to the Nevada statute give a controlling stockholder a presumption of no fiduciary breach on a transaction in which the controller has a material financial interest; and officers can be exculpated in derivative actions, which Delaware does not permit. The proxy states the effect plainly: the conversion "will generally result in … the elimination of any liability of an officer or director for a breach of fiduciary duty, unless arising from intentional misconduct, fraud or a knowing violation of law." The sequence is worth recording: at the 2025 annual meeting stockholders approved a Delaware certificate adding officer exculpation to the fullest extent Delaware allowed, and ten months later the company moved to a state where that protection is broader. The proxy discloses the conflict and states that no changes to founder arrangements are "currently under consideration" as of February 2026, which describes the position in February 2026 and promises nothing. At the 2026 annual meeting the board recommended against a shareholder proposal replacing all supermajority requirements with simple-majority voting.

Founder selling: All executive and director selling runs through Rule 10b5-1 plans adopted annually. Pomel's discretionary selling is roughly 1.0-1.2m shares a year net of sell-to-cover; Lê-Quôc adopted a plan on 2026-06-15 for up to 1,332,312 shares with no sell-to-cover carve-out disclosed, 14% larger than his prior plan at a share price that had roughly doubled, and that plan was disclosed in the same 10-Q that first disclosed the largest customer's usage reduction. Reported beneficial ownership declined 73.1% for Pomel and 62.8% for Lê-Quôc over six years, from 39.2m and 24.6m shares (2020-03-31) to 10.5m and 9.2m (2026-03-31), worth roughly $3.1bn and $1.7bn of dispositions [estimate: period-by-period decline in reported beneficial ownership valued at the average closing price between proxy record dates; a lower bound, because the change nets new vesting against sales and option exercises inside the 60-day window move the reported figure]. The retained stakes are still worth about $2.7bn and $2.35bn at the 2026-08-10 price. The sales were programmatic and spread evenly across a period whose average price of $111.74 is well below the current price.

Every per-share line grows about three to four points a year slower than its absolute counterpart, so roughly one eighth of the compounding went to employees. Two figures inside FY2025 sharpen it: free cash flow less total stock compensation was $140.6m in FY2025, down from $191.6m in FY2024, even though free cash flow rose 18.0%, because total stock compensation grew 32.7%. First-half 2026 improved sharply on the same basis, to $134.6m against $53.4m, and the improvement came from revenue accelerating.

Dilution has run at or above target for three years. Net dilution on ending shares was 3.20% (2020), 2.45%, 1.86%, 3.73% (2023), 3.33%, 3.04% (2025) and 1.82% in the first half of 2026, against a target of 2.5-3.5% set in 2024 and tightened to 2.5-3.0% in 2026. Management has never stated which share basis the target uses, and the three plausible bases give different answers. Cumulatively, 62.6m shares were issued FY2020 through 1H2026, worth $7,188m at the respective years' average prices against $3,542m of cumulative free cash flow [estimate: shares issued per each year's equity statement × the arithmetic mean of that calendar year's daily closes; using each year's low instead gives $4,748m and each year's high $10,364m]. Valued at the 2026-08-10 close those shares are worth $16,082m. Composition in FY2025: 87% of issuance was compensation and the remainder acquisition currency, and the option channel is nearly exhausted, with options outstanding down from 36.4m at 2019-12-31 to 3.47m at 2025-12-31 at a $7.26 average strike and none granted since FY2020. From here dilution is almost all RSUs and PSUs, and the committed pipeline is $2,078.3m of unrecognised compensation over a weighted-average 2.8 years, roughly $742m a year before a single new grant.

Reported stock compensation understates what shareholders gave up. Expense is measured at grant-date fair value; the RSUs that vested in FY2025 had a weighted-average grant fair value of $113.50 against a FY2025 average market price of $133.44, and options exercised in FY2025 had a $1.84 weighted-average strike and produced $429.8m of intrinsic value. Aggregate option-exercise intrinsic value FY2021-FY2025 was $2,505.7m. Across FY2020 through 1H2026 the market value of shares delivered was 2.55x the reported expense.

In FY2023 and FY2025 the entire GAAP profit came from the securities portfolio and more, because the operating business lost money on a GAAP basis in both years. 11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Datadog is a disciplined acqui-hirer whose program has built real product lines with small amounts of capital, and the financial statements are structurally incapable of grading it. Twenty business combinations closed between the September 2019 IPO and 30 June 2026 for roughly $738m of cash and stock, against $914.7m of free cash flow in FY2025 alone. Seven of the acquired technologies are named products on the current platform map: Observability Pipelines (Timber), Code Security (Hdiv and Codiga), CI Visibility and Test Optimization (Undefined Labs), Data Observability (Metaplane), Product Analytics and Experiments (Eppo), and Cloudcraft. The Sqreen technology shipped as Application Security Management in 2022 and belongs to a security suite that passed $100m of ARR. Three produced nothing that survives: CoScreen was shut down on 2026-07-31, Seekret's API observability has no named product and was last mentioned in Q4 2022, and Actiondesk was described once in December 2023 and never again. Datadog has never divested a business, and no period carries a discontinued-operations line.

Three things qualify that record. First, the accounts cannot distinguish a success from a failure here. Datadog has never impaired a dollar of goodwill in any year from 2018 through mid-2026 across $696m of post-IPO goodwill additions, and every 10-K states so explicitly. An acqui-hire books almost everything to goodwill — $60.5m of identifiable intangibles against $696m of goodwill, 8.0% of the total — because an assembled workforce is not a recognisable intangible, and goodwill is then tested at a single reporting unit whose fair value is the whole company. A failed $40m tuck-in cannot show up. That leaves the product record as the test. Second, the booked purchase price understates what the deals cost. Management announced Sqreen at "$260 million" of total transaction costs with approximately 25% deferred in cash and stock; the purchase-price allocation records $219.4m, a $40.6m gap, and the filing never explains it. Press reporting put Eppo alone at a planned $220m while the entire FY2025 aggregate for three deals was $178.4m [techcrunch.com, accessed 2026-08-10] [web]. Retention and earn-out consideration contingent on continued service is excluded from purchase price under ASC 805 and lands in operating expense and stock compensation instead, so the true cost is larger than the goodwill record shows and is not separately disclosed. Third, the program has stepped up hard. First-half 2026 recorded $191.5m of consideration and $178.7m of goodwill in six months, more than all of FY2025 and more than 2022, 2023 and 2024 combined on goodwill, and the two named 2026 targets are AI research and agent capability.

Goodwill went $17.6m (2020) → $292.2m (2021) → $352.7m (2023) → $530.6m (2025) → $706.7m (2026-06-30), 9.4% of total assets, and rose 33.2% in the six months to June 2026. Amortisation of acquired intangibles was $6.5m in FY2025, 0.19% of revenue. Identifiable intangibles are 8.0% of goodwill-plus-intangibles recorded since the IPO, which is what the strategy looks like in the accounts: "we are not acquiring companies to run as stand-alone platforms … what we are doing is largely acquiring talented R&D teams" (Investor Day 2022).

Multiples are not derivable. What the stock was worth when Datadog paid in it is. Datadog's own enterprise value against trailing revenue on the day each named deal was announced or closed: 57.9x at the Sqreen and Timber announcement (2021-02-11), 17.1x at Quickwit (2025-01-08), 12.0x at Eppo (2025-05-05), 13.0x at Propolis (2026-01-29) and 24.2x when Adaptive ML closed (2026-06-30). The largest deal in the record was paid partly in stock issued when Datadog's own trailing multiple was roughly 3-5x the level at which the 2025 and 2026 stock consideration was issued. Implied issue prices on the restricted shares — $68.88 in FY2025 and about $98.80 in 1H 2026 — are below the market price prevailing in those quarters, consistent with a discount for the restriction.

Datadog answered structural consolidation with acqui-hires, and it did so knowingly. The largest deal in seven years is Sqreen at $219.4m, 0.6% of Datadog's enterprise value on the announcement date. Over the same window Cisco bought Splunk for roughly $28bn and Palo Alto Networks bought Chronosphere for $3.35bn. Asked directly on the Q1 2024 call whether $1bn of annual operating cash flow argued for going bigger, Pomel opened with "everything is on the table for us. Like we're very busy on the M&A side. We have a team that is, at any point in time, reviewing multiple deals," and closed with "that opens a number of doors for us, and we fully intend to use that if we have the right opportunity", while adding that "the larger the acquisition, the less likely it is to happen because we're extremely selective." The record is selectivity, and no large acquisition has been done.

Weighted-average cost of debt. One instrument, so the weighted average is that instrument. Principal-weighted contractual coupon: 0.00%. GAAP effective rate, which is amortization of issuance costs only: 0.43%. All-in economic cost including the capped-call premium: 2.65%, the internal rate of return from $878.2m of net cash raised ($979.1m of proceeds less $100.9m of capped calls) to a $1,000.0m repayment 4.97 years later, assuming cash settlement at par and the capped calls expiring worthless.

Even at the all-in figure, Datadog financed roughly 173 basis points inside the 4.382% five-year Treasury of December 2024, and 438 basis points inside on a cash-coupon basis. The economic cost sits entirely in the conversion option written to noteholders, and Datadog bought most of that back for $100.9m, which is why the capped-call cost belongs in the calculation even though GAAP records it as a reduction of paid-in capital.

The 2025 notes are the precedent for how the 2029 notes will likely be handled. The entire $747.5m financing produced a net share effect of minus 6,169 shares — the equity statement records the line as "Settlement of capped calls related to 2025 Convertible Senior Notes — (6,169)". All-in cash cost across the life was $137.0m on $747.5m borrowed over five years, or roughly 0.6% a year including the coupon, with zero net equity issued.

GAAP overstates this. The diluted denominator uses the if-converted method and adds the full 4,596 thousand shares while excluding the capped calls as anti-dilutive, so the Q2 2026 diluted count of 371,023 thousand contains 4,596 thousand shares — 1.24% of the count — whose real dilution is zero at any price up to $322.38. If Datadog instead settled entirely in shares it would issue 4,595,500 and keep the $1,000m of cash; at the current price the capped calls return 697,000, for a net 3,898,500 shares, or 1.09%.

One live mechanical item: If the stock closes at or above $282.88 for 20 of any 30 consecutive trading days ending on a quarter's last trading day, $1.0bn moves from non-current to current liabilities, taking the current ratio from 3.2x to 2.1x. Q3 2026 has two such closes to date, on 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-05, out of 28 sessions, before the 19.0% decline on the Q2 print. The condition is live but far from met, and meeting it would require no cash.

Counterparty exposure: The capped calls are uncollateralized claims on unnamed bank counterparties, and the 10-K flags it: "Our exposure to the credit risk of the option counterparties will not be secured by any collateral." Intrinsic exposure at the 2026-08-10 close is 4,595,500 shares × ($256.50 − $217.60) = $178.8m, and the full mark-to-market including time value is higher, on a stock with 90-day realized volatility of 79.9%.

No filing explains the step. Purchase commitments went $485.0m (2023-12-31) → $1,400m (2024-12-31), a 2.9x increase, in the year the AI-native cohort was scaling and the December 2024 convertible was issued.

Cumulative since 2019-12-31: +62,569,835 shares, +21.1%, a 2.95% compound annual rate over six and a half years. Gross issuance was 62,576,004 and the only offset in the entire history is the 6,169-share receipt from the capped-call settlement. Excluding acquisition consideration, organic 1H2026 dilution was 5,680,190 shares, or 1.61% in six months, a roughly 3.2% annual pace.

One measure has inflected in Datadog's favour. Stock compensation was 19.6% of revenue in Q2 2026 against 21.8% a year earlier and 21.9% for FY2025, the first sustained leverage in the company's history and the first sub-20% reading since 2021.▪ The pool grew slower than revenue: the unvested RSU and PSU pool moved from 16,700,043 at 2025-12-31 to 17,099,356 at 2026-06-30, up 2.4%, while revenue grew 34%, and annualised 1H2026 grant value of $1,337m compares with FY2025's $1,275m, roughly flat while revenue grows a third. Whether it holds is the open question, because a denominator effect reverses when growth normalises.

Private-sector credit — corporate bonds, commercial paper and certificates of deposit — is $3,793.1m, or 76.1% of total liquidity, against $757.4m of US government paper. Gross unrealized losses widened from $137k at 2025-12-31 to $9,490k at 2026-06-30, and the portfolio moved from a net unrealized gain of $8,365k to a net unrealized loss of $8,714k. At 0.19% of the portfolio that is immaterial in size, and it is the first period since the portfolio reached this scale in which it is underwater. Datadog does not disclose a credit-rating distribution, a single-issuer concentration limit, or an investment policy, and management's only assurance is that unrealized losses are not credit-related. The portfolio produced 159% of FY2025 GAAP net income and is three-quarters corporate credit.

12.6 Structural balance-sheet risks, ranked

  1. Dilution trajectory, 3.0-3.7% a year on ending shares against a 2.5-3.0% target, with no buyback in seven years. Trigger: growth normalising while dollar grant value holds, which reverses the falling intensity in Section 12.4.
  2. Interest-income dependence, $171.4m of other income in FY2025 against a $44.4m GAAP operating loss. Trigger: rate cuts; Section 10.6 sizes 100 basis points at roughly $50m, or 46% of FY2025 GAAP net income. Item 7A treats a 10% relative rate move — roughly $21m pre-tax, or 19.5% of FY2025 GAAP net income — as immaterial.
  3. Credit concentration inside the cash pile, 76.1% of $4,985.4m in corporate credit, larger than the debt itself. Trigger: an issuer default or spread widening, against no disclosed rating distribution or issuer limit.
  4. Conversion-trigger reclassification. Trigger: twenty closes at or above $282.88 in thirty trading days ending a quarter, which moves $1.0bn to current liabilities and can prompt holder conversions Datadog must then settle.
  5. Capped-call counterparty risk, $178.8m of intrinsic uncollateralized exposure. Trigger: failure of an unnamed bank counterparty, with exposure rising in both price and volatility.
  6. Purchase commitments against a revenue slowdown, $1.4bn over five years against $380-550m of annual hosting spend. Trigger: a usage decline deep enough to leave committed capacity unused.
  7. Conversion overhang, the smallest of these. Trigger: a price far above the $322.38 cap; net dilution is zero below it and 0.45% of shares at $500.

Two disagreements inside the filings are unresolved. The FY2025 10-K reports contractual interest expense of zero for the year while the Q2 2026 10-Q reports $364k for the six months ended 2025-06-30 on the same instrument, which bore a 0.125% coupon payable each June 15 and matured 2025-06-15. And the notes footnote total of $5,602k in FY2025 does not tie to income-statement interest expense of $11,059k, with the $5,457k residual unexplained anywhere in the filing. Both are immaterial in magnitude and both are direct disagreements between disclosures on the same period.

Forward columns are Bloomberg BEst consensus as of 2026-08-10 and nothing is bridged from any model. Consensus gross profit, operating income, EBITDA, net income and EPS are on the non-GAAP basis Datadog guides to, so no consensus GAAP operating income exists and those cells are empty; consensus GAAP EPS is published separately and is shown. Bloomberg publishes no consensus operating cash flow, capitalized software, buyback, dividend, return or net-cash line for this name, which is why those cells are empty, and its capex line excludes capitalized software, which is why forward capex intensity of 1.4-1.7% sits far below the 4-5% of revenue management guides for the two combined. Growth rows print n/m where the prior-year base is at or below zero. Capex/EBITDA uses stock-comp-excluded EBITDA for actual years and consensus EBITDA for forward years. Net debt/EBITDA is signed, so negative means net cash, and it uses stock-comp-excluded EBITDA. GAAP return on invested capital is negative in six of seven years because the numerator is a GAAP operating loss and the denominator nets a $4.5bn securities portfolio; the economically meaningful measure is the 17.1% R&D-capitalized figure in Section 3.4. Non-GAAP diluted EPS growth for FY2023 sits on a basis break: Datadog adopted an assumed 21% non-GAAP tax rate with the Q4 2023 release and restated FY2022 to $0.80 from the $0.97 its own quarterly releases sum to, so the +35% shown understates the like-for-like rate by roughly 20 points.

The gap between the two operating-income series is roughly the whole of operating profit. In FY2025, stock compensation of $750.7m was 21.9% of revenue against a GAAP operating loss of $44.4m: the non-GAAP series alone shows a business earning a 22.4% operating margin, the GAAP series alone shows a business that has earned a full-year operating profit exactly once, and both statements are true of the same year. Two thirds of the charge is booked in research and development: reported R&D of $1,548.5m contains $469.5m of stock compensation, so cash R&D was $1,078.9m, or 31.5% of revenue against the reported 45.2%.

Margin bridge: From FY2023 to FY2024 the GAAP operating margin improved 360 basis points as gross margin added 10, R&D took out 230, S&M 40 and G&A 90. It is the only year in the series with clean GAAP operating leverage. From FY2024 to FY2025 it reversed 330 basis points: gross margin −80, R&D +230, S&M −30, G&A +60, with R&D growing 34.3% against revenue growth of 27.7% and G&A growing 36.3%. The deterioration is not a stock-compensation artefact, because the ex-SBC margin still declined 270 basis points. From 1H2025 to 1H2026 the GAAP margin improved 360 basis points as every operating expense line reverted to leverage while gross margin kept deteriorating.

Growth is organic. Datadog does not disclose acquired revenue and states in each 10-K that "Pro forma results of operations from the acquisitions have not been presented because they were not material to the consolidated results of operations." Cash paid for acquisitions never exceeded $226.5m in a year and was under $50m in five of seven. Treat the whole series as organic, with one caveat: FY2021 goodwill rose $275.2m, so FY2021 and FY2022 contain an unquantified acquired contribution the company deemed immaterial.

International share peaked at 30.2% in FY2024 and declined to 29.0% in FY2025, then to 27% of 1H 2026 revenue. FY2025 is the first year since FY2019 in which North America outgrew International, and the mechanism is the AI-native cohort's US concentration: US revenue share rose from 66.5% to 67.7% in the same year.

Working capital funds the business. Deferred revenue grew $273.3m in FY2025 alone and has run 33-38% of revenue for seven years with no trend. Days sales outstanding improved 24 days across the seven years, from 103.0 to 78.9. Free cash flow conversion against stock-comp-excluded operating income has exceeded 100% in every year since FY2020 and averaged 135.6%, for two reasons that are not margins: customers pay in advance, and stock compensation is a non-cash charge free cash flow picks up which the ex-SBC operating income line has already removed. Accounts payable rose from $148.8m at 2025-12-31 to $313.5m at 2026-06-30, contributing a $155.1m source of cash against $85.6m a year earlier, so $69.5m — 38.8% — of the year-over-year increase in first-half operating cash flow came from that swing alone. Given that the hyperscaler bill is the largest component of cost of revenue, this is most likely payment timing and should reverse.

Accounting notes that matter. Datadog has never restated its accounts, reported a material weakness, or changed accountants. Capitalized software development rose from $34.8m (FY2023) to $85.8m (FY2025), +147% against revenue +61%, and in January 2025 the company extended the estimated useful life of those costs from two years to three, effective FY2025. Free cash flow is unaffected, since both capex and capitalized software are deductions, but GAAP research expense and GAAP operating income are flattered in FY2025, the year GAAP operating income turned negative. A full valuation allowance sits on US federal and state deferred tax assets, with an $86.6m net increase in FY2025 against a $42.8m tax at the statutory rate, so the effective rate is not economically meaningful in any year; cash taxes paid were $17.6m (FY2025), $21.0m (FY2024) and $16.5m (FY2023).

Every trailing-four-quarter sum ties exactly to the annual series on revenue, gross profit, GAAP operating income, net income, operating cash flow, capex, capitalized software, free cash flow and stock compensation; the only difference anywhere is $1 thousand of rounding inside the Q4 2025 release's own non-GAAP operating income columns.

Three inflections against FY2025:

  • Revenue growth accelerated to +35.6%, the fastest since Q4 2022, adding $294.7m year over year. Both parts contributed: management said growth excluding AI-native customers reached "the high 20s" against 18% a year earlier, and the cohort contributed high single digit percentage points. The same filing discloses the largest customer's usage reduction beginning Q3 2026, already inside Q3 and full-year guidance.
  • Gross margin at 78.6% is the lowest quarterly figure since Q3 2022, down 130 basis points year over year and 360 from the Q4 2023 peak, with $64.1m of the $74.1m quarterly cost-of-revenue increase attributed to third-party cloud hosting and software. Management's framing is that gross margin "has been in the 80% plus or minus range historically" with "no change in our expectations"; the reported series has now printed below 80% in four of the last six quarters and declined in each of the last two.
  • Remaining performance obligations went flat. RPO moved $3,461.2m → $3,484.4m → $3,471.4m, +0.3% across two quarters against +6.7% over the equivalent two quarters of 2025, while year-over-year RPO is still +43% and billings grew 38% in Q2 2026, faster than revenue. Collections are not the issue, so the difference is contract duration and renewal timing. Management pre-empts the question each quarter — "we continue to believe revenue is a better indicator of our business trends than billings and RPO given their variability".

The inflections these metrics reveal, each with its driver:

  • Net retention is the cycle indicator and it has run one full round trip. Above 130% for 23 consecutive quarters through Q1 2023, then mid-110%'s at the 2023 trough, then back to low-120%'s at 2026-06-30. The driver in both directions was usage growth per existing customer. Datadog is the only one of the three listed pure-plays to have completed a decay-and-recovery cycle; Dynatrace and Elastic left the 120s and settled at 110-112% without re-accelerating.
  • The $100k+ cohort re-accelerated after two flat years and now supplies most of the growth. Growth ran 14.7% and 13.2% in FY2023 and FY2024 before rising to 19.4% in FY2025 and 22.6% year over year at Q2 2026, six consecutive quarters of acceleration, and that cohort holds 91% of ARR. The $1m+ count decelerated a full year later than revenue did — +47%, +25%, +17%, then +31%, which is disclosed annually and easy to miss.
  • The land motion is the metric that broke. Net customer adds were +200 in Q2 2026 against a 500-900 range and 900 in the same quarter a year earlier, and year-over-year customer growth halved from 9.9% to 6.4% in eighteen months. Management attributes it to the free-tier boundary; Risk 9 in Section 18 sets out the evidence on both sides.
  • Multi-product attach inflected upward in the twelve months to June 2026. The 6+, 8+ and 10+ buckets each rose 6-8 points after years of 2-4 point annual moves, while the 2+ bucket added one point. Every dollar of that comes from the products a customer already had access to on an installed agent, which is why the attach series and the retention series move together.
  • Discontinued: dollar-based net retention above 130%, published in the 2021 deck as sustained for 16 consecutive quarters, is now disclosed only as a band and is not a target in any deck. And a metric management still publishes but stopped leading with: the 2+ product figure was the headline platform proof from 2019 to 2024 and the prepared remarks have led with the 4+ figure since Q1 2026.
  • A new line with a short history: the AI-native cohort's share of revenue, published for 2021-2025 only in the February 2026 deck, at 1%, 1%, 2%, 5% and 11%.

14. Expectations: internal against external against base rates

Management and the street differ little on the numbers and a great deal on the reasons. Consensus revenue for FY2026 of $4,469m is 0.2% above the guide midpoint and FY2027 of $5,481m implies +22.6%, while Datadog's own record of beating its post-Q2 full-year guide by 2.2-3.6% would put FY2026 at $4.55-4.62bn. Where management and the street diverge is gross margin: the company gives no gross-margin guidance at all, and consensus assumes the decline reverses 70 basis points within two quarters and never resumes.▪
