That specific call was wrong at the time of writing Datadog's own 2022-23 episode: 57 points of deceleration over five quarters, six quarters from onset to moderation
Non-GAAP gross margin No guidance is given. "80% plus or minus", "no change in our expectations" 80.1% (FY2026), 80.4%, 80.3%, 80.5% (FY2029) 1H 2026 was 79.9% with a 79.6% Q2 exit, so the consensus FY2026 requires the second half to average 80.3%, seventy basis points above the Q2 level, with nothing to anchor it. Consensus has already been cut 103bp on FY2026, 98bp on FY2027 and 111bp on FY2028 over fourteen months and reset flat each time Rented-cloud observability cohort settles at 74-79%, central ~77%; Datadog's 80% is at the class ceiling
Non-GAAP operating margin 25%+ long term, no date; FY2026 implies 22.9% 23.0% (FY2026), 23.6%, 24.6%, 26.3% (FY2029) Management's own line-item targets sum to about 60% of revenue, which caps the margin near 20%. The 25%+ goal and the line-item targets are inconsistent and neither document reconciles them 1-2 points a year of expansion is the class median while growth exceeds 20%; 22-28% by FY2028, central ~25%
GAAP operating margin Not guided. FY2025 was a $44.4m loss No consensus line published Consensus operating income is non-GAAP throughout, so nobody publishes a GAAP operating margin for this company Investment-stage crossers (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Palo Alto) took four to six years from a negative crossing to a high-single-digit GAAP margin: 3-13% by FY2029-30, central ~7%
Stock-based compensation Not guided; net dilution target 2.5-3.0% ~$940m for FY2026, ~21% of revenue, fully added back Neither publishes an intensity path. The realized 1H2026 rate of 19.6% is 2.2 points below a year earlier The class median five-year change in intensity from a $1bn base is −0.4 points, and the fall to single digits happens between $6bn and $15bn of revenue, not $3-6bn
Free cash flow Not guided; capex plus capitalized software 4-5% of revenue $1,176m (FY2026), 26.3% margin Consensus capex of $63.0m is 1.4% of revenue against the company's 4-5% including capitalized software, because the Bloomberg field excludes capitalized software. Use the guidance Class at $3-6bn of revenue: 26-33%, central ~29%. On free cash flow less stock compensation, 8-18%, central ~12%, against Datadog's 4.8% today

Customer count Not guided No published estimate Growth is coming almost entirely from expansion inside a near-static account base and no estimate reflects it —

14.1 The guidance record

Datadog has beaten its quarterly guidance midpoint on revenue in 27 of 27 quarters, on non-GAAP operating income in 25 of 25 guided quarters, and on non-GAAP EPS in 27 of 27. Every quarter in the record has landed above the guided range. The mean revenue beat against midpoint is +6.0% and the median +4.8%, and it compressed and then stabilised:

Block of eight guides Mean beat Median Range
Q4 2019 – Q3 2021 +8.6% +9.2% +3.7% to +11.4%
Q4 2021 – Q3 2023 +6.0% +5.5% +1.9% to +12.1%
Q4 2023 – Q3 2025 +4.0% +4.0% +3.1% to +4.8%
Last eight (Q3 2024 – Q2 2026) +4.3% +4.3% +3.1% to +5.2%

Accuracy is not degrading; the distribution has stabilised at about four points of embedded cushion per quarter. Full-year guidance walks the same way, and the initial guide stays heavily discounted: FY2020 through FY2025 initial full-year guides were beaten by a mean of +10.1%, and FY2026 is already +9.3% above its initial guide with two quarters unreported.

FY Initial (Q4 print) +1Q +2Q +3Q Actual vs initial vs final

2021 830 885 941 994 1,028.8 +24.0% +3.5%
2022 1,520 1,610 1,620 1,652 1,675.1 +10.2% +1.4%

FY2023 is the only full-year reduction in the record, a $35m cut at the Q2 2023 print during the optimisation slowdown, and the year still finished above every guide issued. The final-quarter guide has become very tight, beaten by only 1.0-1.4% since FY2022 against 2.5-3.5% in 2020-21.

Q1 2025 is the one near-break. Non-GAAP operating income of $166.5m beat a $162-166m guide by $2.5m, the smallest margin in 25 guided quarters, and the cause was disclosed: "our cloud hosting costs rose more quickly than we expected in Q1, as we supported large growth spikes from some of our largest customers." Management then cut the full-year operating income guide from a $665m midpoint to $635m while raising the full-year revenue guide by $40m, the only downward profit revision in the post-IPO record. The same cost mechanism is live again.

14.2 The standing targets, by vintage

Datadog has issued a long-term financial framework twice, in February 2024 and February 2026, plus an IPO-era set disclosed retrospectively in 2024. Only one cell is populated in the current version.

Non-GAAP Goal at IPO (2019) 2026 investor day language FY2025 actual
Gross margin 77-78% "plus or minus 80%" 81%
R&D 22-26% "this has been our target around 30%" 30%
S&M 23-27% "roughly the mid-20s range" 23%
G&A 6-8% "around 5%" 5%
Operating margin 20-25% 25%+, tabled, no date 22%
Net share dilution not set 2.5% to 3.0% (was 2.5-3.5% in 2024) 3.04%

Three targets moved and none was announced as a revision. The research target moved from 22-26% to "around 30%", a permanent four-to-eight-point increase in the intended cost base presented as continuity, and the one target Datadog has never met is presented in the deck as a feature. The gross-margin goal moved up from 77-78% to about 80%. And the dilution target tightened by half a point on the shareholder-friendly side. Progress against the one tabled goal: 23% (2023), 25% (2024), 22% (2025), 22.9% guided (2026) — hit once, in the year before it became the current framework, and guided to be missed for a second consecutive year.

14.3 Where the estimate set is thin

FY2026 is not a forecast: 40 analysts spread across $122m of revenue on a $4.47bn base with a standard deviation of 0.5%. Dispersion opens sharply from FY2027, where the revenue spread is 12.4% of the mean and the non-GAAP EPS spread 58.3%, with the mean 4.4% above the median because a small number of contributors model very high operating leverage on higher revenue. The revenue debate and the margin debate compound in EPS. By FY2029 and FY2030 the set is too thin to be a consensus at all — eight and seven contributors on revenue, four on FY2029 EPS — and consensus FY2028 growth of +22.5% sits above the +21.4% modelled for Q4 2027, so the mean contains a 2028 re-acceleration that no quarterly estimate supports. The outer-year operating and free-cash-flow margins are terminal placeholders.

14.4 What no published estimate reflects

Six drivers the evidence says matter, with no consensus line and no commentary found engaging with them:

  • the marketplace channel's margin effect, now 15% of ARR and modelled nowhere;
  • the $1.4bn of non-cancelable purchase commitments set against usage-based revenue;
  • customer count, nearly flat at +6.4% against 35.6% revenue growth;
  • the divergence between remaining performance obligations and revenue;
  • the Bits AI pricing change to AI credits;
  • infinite-cardinality metrics, launched at DASH in June 2026 and described as letting users "generate larger amounts of data with AI agents without incurring any extra costs", which deliberately decouples data volume from revenue on the metrics product in a usage-based model.

To that list belongs the coupling in Section 6.3: no estimate, internal or external, links Datadog's growth path to hyperscaler consumption growth, against a historical downside beta near 2.3x.

15. Market pricing and valuation history

Datadog began trading on 2019-09-19 after an IPO priced at $27.00, so the price history runs 6.9 years and 1,731 trading sessions. The first close was $37.55, a 39% first-day premium. Datadog has never paid a dividend and the Bloomberg gross-dividend total-return index is identical to the price index on every date in the series, so price return and total return are the same number in every year below.

Why the multiple history leads on EV/Sales. GAAP diluted EPS was negative in FY2019 through FY2022 and below $0.55 in every year since, so a trailing GAAP P/E table shows four blanks and then prints of 867x, 275x and 439x, which describes the accounting. The reason is disclosed: stock compensation of $750.7m in FY2025, 21.9% of revenue, is why FY2025 shows a GAAP operating loss, and GAAP net income of $107.7m exists only because other income was $171.4m. The measures the market used are EV/Sales and, from mid-2021 onward, price to forward non-GAAP EPS.

Eight of the last twelve reactions exceeded ±5% and the mean absolute reaction was 12.1%. The reaction correlates with the forward guide. The 2021 peak and the 2022 de-rating. The price peaked at $196.56 on 2021-11-09 at 44.9x forward sales, but the multiple had peaked thirteen months earlier at 47.4x on 2020-10-13 when the price was $116.87; between those dates the price rose 68% and the multiple declined 5%, so consensus forward revenue did all the work. From the November 2021 peak to the April 2023 trough of $62.69 the price declined 68.1% while the twelve-month-forward consensus revenue estimate rose 68.4%, from $1,351m to $2,276m, and EV/forward sales compressed 81.4%. Nothing in the revenue estimates explains that decline; it compressed alongside the whole complex, with IGV down 20-28% in each leg and the Nasdaq 100 down 24.3% in the largest.

The 2023 optimisation trough is the only episode in the seven-year record where the forward consensus revenue estimate stopped rising, moving −0.1% while IGV declined 1.9% and the Nasdaq 100 was flat. That leg was Datadog's own, and the mechanism is in the calls: the FY2023 guide was cut on 2023-08-08 and the shares declined 17.2% that session with IGV −1.6%. Growth had decelerated from 83% in Q1 2022 to 25% in Q2 2023.

The 2024-25 and 2025-26 drawdowns are the same shape and neither involved an estimate cut. Each saw the price decline roughly 48% while forward consensus revenue rose 5.1% and the multiple compressed more than 52%. The 2026-02-23 session itself, −11.3% for Datadog, was not a company event: MongoDB declined 11.4%, Snowflake 8.6%, Dynatrace 5.1% and IGV 4.8% against a Nasdaq 100 down 1.2%.

The 2026-08-06 session. The Q2 2026 release beat on everything and raised everything: revenue $1,121.5m, +36% and 3.9% above consensus; non-GAAP EPS $0.65 against $0.597; a Q3 revenue guide whose midpoint was 3.0% above the consensus standing the day before; and a full-year guide raised on revenue, operating income and EPS. Consensus moved up on the print — FY2026 revenue consensus from $4,350.8m to $4,469.1m (+2.7%), FY2027 from $5,292.8m to $5,480.9m (+3.6%), and every forward quarter's estimate rose. The shares declined 19.0%, from $283.17 to $229.29, as EV to twelve-month-forward consensus sales went from 19.8x to 15.6x, a 21.1% multiple compression in one session against IGV −1.9% and the Nasdaq 100 −0.4%.

What the market reacted to is the composition of the guide. The Q3 guide midpoint of $1,140m is $18.5m above Q2's $1,121.5m, a 1.7% sequential increase, against Q2-to-Q3 increases of 7.5% (2023), 7.0% (2024) and 7.1% (2025), and against management's own framing a quarter earlier of "sequential revenue growth of $64 million to $74 million or 6% to 7%." On a year-over-year basis the guide steps from 36% delivered to 28-29% guided in a company that had just posted five consecutive quarters of acceleration. Management put the counter-fact on the same call — "if you back out our largest customer from our growth, you get pretty much the same growth rate as the rest of the business has been accelerating very steadily", and both facts stand together. The market repriced the multiple. By 2026-08-10 the shares had recovered to $257.26, so 52% of the one-session decline was retraced within two sessions.

The table uses two conventions. Fiscal-year labels, not calendar dates: "2026E" is the fiscal year Bloomberg labels 2026, which ends 2026-06-30 for Microsoft and Atlassian, in early 2026 for Snowflake and CrowdStrike, 2026-03-31 for Dynatrace and 2026-04-30 for Elastic, so the columns are not all as of the same calendar date. That is inherent to a multi-year-end comp set. The two index rows are on a different estimate basis: the indices ignore the absolute fiscal-year override and answer only the rolling blended-forward codes, so their 2026E/2027E/2028E cells are one-, two- and three-year blends, and their revision, enterprise-value and net-debt cells are left blank.

FY2025 adjusted and GAAP EPS are reported actuals, because Bloomberg freezes the pre-report estimate instead of overwriting it. GAAP P/E prints n/m where GAAP EPS is at or below $0.10 while the GAAP EPS value itself is kept, which is why Datadog's 502x GAAP 2026E figure sits beside Atlassian's, Snowflake's and Elastic's n/m. Four names were omitted, with the reason for each: New Relic (private since November 2023), Splunk (acquired by Cisco; its economics are visible only inside Cisco's Security and Observability lines), SolarWinds (taken private 2025-04-16, Form 15 filed 2025-04-28, absent from the SEC ticker file), and Confluent, which Bloomberg now reports with an acquired market status, no current price and a last daily price of $30.99 on 2026-03-16. Confluent was a live public comp when this peer list was drawn and is not one now; the acquirer is not established from the terminal. Grafana Labs and Chronosphere have never been public.

17. Forward model summary

Three scenarios run from FY2025 actuals through FY2033, projecting revenue to free cash flow, both operating-income bases, and the share count off the compensation and convertible assumptions.

17.1 The model is built on cohorts, not a growth rate

Datadog's growth has changed shape and a top-down revenue rate would hide the change. Customer count growth has declined to +6.4% while revenue grew +35.6%, so almost all growth now arrives as more spend inside a nearly static account base:

Date Customers YoY Estimated total ARR ARR per customer YoY
2019-12-31 10,500 — $477m $45.4k —
2021-12-31 18,800 +32.4% $1,352m $71.9k +38.5%
2023-12-31 27,300 +17.7% $2,382m $87.3k +6.9%
2024-12-31 30,000 +9.9% $2,980m $99.4k +13.9%
2025-12-31 32,700 +9.0% $3,851m $117.8k +18.5%
2026-06-30 33,400 +6.4% $4,531m $135.6k +27.4%

[estimate: total ARR taken as Q4 revenue × 4.04, which reproduces the independent month-end-MRR method within 0.5% at every year end; fiscal-year revenue is then the mean of opening and closing ARR × 1.003, which reproduces FY2024 within +0.2% and FY2025 within 0.0%. The identity assumes smooth growth within the year and is therefore not used for FY2026, where growth is front-loaded.]

The driver tree splits ARR three ways and models each separately, so the live issue is handled as two facts:

Revenue ├── BASE BUSINESS (non-AI-native) 89.5% of FY2025 ARR │ ARR_base(t) = ARR_base(t−1) × NRR_base(t) + ARR_base(t−1) × newlogo_pct(t) │ ├── NRR_base ← multi-product attach, usage growth per product, price/discount │ └── newlogo_pct ← gross new logos × average land ARR, cross-checked to net customer adds ├── AI-NATIVE COHORT excluding the largest customer 6.6% of FY2025 ARR │ └── ultimate exposure: capital raised by AI labs × share spent on compute │ × share of that compute they instrument └── LARGEST CUSTOMER 3.9% of FY2025 ARR └── a disclosed usage reduction begins Q3 2026

Cohort ARR anchors, the largest source of error in the revenue build:

Date Total ARR Base business AI-native ex-largest Largest customer
2024-12-31 $2,980m $2,801m $109m $70m
2025-12-31 $3,851m $3,447m $254m $150m
2026-06-30 $4,531m $3,897m $414m $220m

[estimate: cohort ARR = disclosed cohort revenue share × quarterly revenue × 4.04, using ~6% of Q4 2024 revenue, ~10.5% of Q4 2025 derived from the 10-K's seven-percentage-point growth contribution, and ~14% of Q2 2026 derived from the disclosed 11% Q2 2025 share plus the 10-Q's high-single-digit contribution. The largest customer is set at $150m and $220m inside the $150-300m band in Section 1.6.] The resulting base-book growth back-tests: base ARR grew 23.1% in FY2025, decomposing as base net retention of 117% plus a new-logo layer of 6.1% of opening ARR, which reconciles both to the disclosed total net retention of about 120% and to new customers supplying 25% of the FY2025 revenue increase.

Two constraints stop the scenarios running away. An incremental-margin governor allows no forecast year an incremental non-GAAP operating margin above Datadog's own best realised year of 36.2% (FY2023); it binds in no base year, which peaks at 31.0%, and in no bull year, which peaks at 36.1%. A gross-margin floor and cap at 72.0% and 81.5% on a GAAP basis stops the hosting cost mechanism compounding indefinitely; the floor binds in the bear from FY2029 and the cap in the bull from FY2029, and neither binds in the base.

Realised Q2-to-Q3 growth was +7.5%, +7.5%, +6.9% and +7.1% in 2022 through 2025 and Q3-to-Q4 +7.5%, +7.7%, +6.9% and +7.6%, so every scenario embeds a real step-down. The base takes a +2.5% beat on the Q3 guide against a trailing-eight-quarter mean of +4.25% — a half-size beat, on the reasoning that the cushion is the usual size but for the first time it is earmarked against a disclosed, already-occurring reduction. The bear would be the first quarter in 27 to land inside the guided range instead of above it. Base non-GAAP operating income of $1,023m falls inside the guided $1,010-1,030m even though base revenue is $66m above the guide midpoint, which is deliberate: the operating-income beat has compressed to a 10.2% median across the last eight quarters because Datadog spends the revenue upside.

17.4 The gross-margin mechanism

Cost of revenue is built in three pieces:

COGS = hosting + other cost of revenue + marketplace channel drag hosting(t) = hosting(t−1) × (1 + telemetry volume growth) × (1 + unit cost change) telemetry volume growth = revenue growth + wedge

The wedge is structural. Infinite-cardinality metrics, launched at DASH in June 2026, let customers "generate larger amounts of data with AI agents without incurring any extra costs", and Flex Logs prices retained data at $0.60 per million events against $1.70 for standard indexing, a 2.8x step down on data Datadog still stores. Both push volume growth above revenue growth by design. The resulting base path, in points of revenue:

FY2025 FY2026 FY2027 FY2028 FY2029 FY2030 FY2031 FY2032 FY2033
Third-party cloud hosting 15.0% 17.6% 18.4% 18.6% 18.6% 18.4% 18.1% 17.6% 17.2%
Telemetry volume index (FY2025 = 1.00) 1.00 1.63 2.21 2.88 3.59 4.35 5.13 5.92 6.76
Hosting cost per telemetry unit index 1.00 0.95 0.90 0.86 0.81 0.77 0.74 0.70 0.66
GAAP gross margin 80.0% 78.3% 77.4% 77.1% 77.2% 77.4% 77.8% 78.3% 78.8%

Gross margin declines for three more years and then recovers as the wedge narrows while unit cost keeps falling. That shape differs from consensus, which has non-GAAP gross margin recovering 70 basis points within two quarters and then flat at 80.3-80.5% through FY2029 with no channel-mix term at all.

Two of the assumptions behind that path do not reproduce from the model's own inputs, and both are flagged here because the gross-margin line is the second-largest driver of the terminal result. The FY2026 telemetry wedge of 31 points was calibrated from the disclosed first-half cost data, but on the model's own FY2025 hosting level of $515m — 75% of cost of revenue — the disclosed $106.0m first-half increase is +43.7% hosting growth against +34.0% revenue growth, a wedge of 17 points, not 31. Recovering 31 requires a hosting share of cost of revenue the model does not use. FY2026 hosting comes out at 17.6% of revenue against 16.2% rebuilt on the model's own hosting level and 16.4% realised in the half, so the second half must run at 18.7% with nothing disclosed to support it. That overstates the drag by roughly 1.4 points of revenue, about $67m of FY2026 gross profit, and it compounds. In the other direction, the FY2027 wedge of 12 points sits below every realised reading in the series — roughly 21 points in FY2025 and 17 in FY2026 on a consistent basis — in the year immediately after the highest reading, and the stated reason (the largest customer's capacity build annualising out) does not apply to the two 2026 product launches that widen the wedge by design. The evidence supports 16-22 points for FY2027, and the difference between 12 and 18 is roughly 0.9 points of FY2027 gross margin, about $50m of gross profit. The two errors run in opposite directions and partly offset, which is why rebuilding on a consistent basis lands FY2027 non-GAAP gross margin within about a point of the 78.2% shown. The level survives; the mechanism does not reproduce. The FY2026-27 margin path is right for compensating reasons.

17.5 Stock compensation, share count and the two profit lines

FY2025 fact pattern: stock compensation of $750.7m net of capitalised amounts, 21.9% of revenue, against a GAAP operating loss of $44.4m. The mechanism modelled is that Datadog holds dollar grant value roughly flat while revenue grows, on the grant-value evidence in Section 12.4. The base extends dollar growth at a decaying rate from 14% to 8%, taking intensity from 21.9% to 12.9% by FY2033.

That is faster than the reference class and it is the model's most aggressive cost assumption on its face, at 1.1 points a year against a class median of 0.08 points. Conditioning the class on companies that scaled, which is what the base case assumes, gives a different picture: Splunk went 27.4% to 21.6% over five years (−1.16 points a year), ServiceNow 25.6% to 19.3% (−1.26), Palo Alto 28.5% to 21.0% (−1.50) and Twilio 23.3% to 13.8% (−1.90), so the base at −1.13 is slower than all four. The cross-sectional check agrees: the base puts revenue at $13.4bn by FY2033, inside the $6-15bn band whose median intensity is 9.7%, so 12.9% is above the band median. The realised 1H2026 rate is already −2.2 points year over year. The assumption is defensible and probably conservative; the residual concern is that the whole mechanism depends on one half-year of grant data. A committed floor applies either way: $2,078.3m of unrecognised compensation on awards already granted at 2026-06-30, over a weighted-average 2.8 years, is roughly $742m a year before a single new grant.

Share count: No repurchase appears in financing activities in any of the seven post-IPO 10-Ks, so every share issued is permanent. Ending shares grow at the modelled net dilution rate, base 3.0% in FY2026 decaying to 1.9% by FY2033 against a management target of 2.5-3.0% and realised 3.0-3.7% over the last three years. The dilution assumption is weak in both directions. The base assumes management hits a target missed for three consecutive years, and Datadog's own FY2026 diluted-share guidance of ~376m against FY2025's 363,472k implies +3.44%, above every scenario. The bear at 3.2% is merely today's pace and does not model the price dependence: dilution from share-settled compensation issues more shares at a lower price, so on roughly $1.2-1.3bn of annual grant value a price 40% below the base path issues about 67% more shares, adding roughly 0.9 points. A coherent bear is 4.0-4.5%. That matters because the bear already shows no GAAP operating profit in eight years, so understated bear dilution understates the per-share damage.

Convertible settlement: The $1.0bn 0.00% notes are assumed settled in cash at the 2029-12-01 maturity, funded from a cash balance that still stands at $7.5bn (bear), $9.5bn (base) or $11.0bn (bull) at the end of FY2029 after the outflow. With combination settlement the capped calls neutralise dilution at every price up to $322.38, so net new shares are zero in bear and base, and the bull adds 1.6m on the assumption the stock is above the cap. The 2025 notes precedent settled at minus 6,169 shares on a $747.5m financing.

With no repurchase the base case accumulates $20.9bn of cash and securities by FY2033 and $625m of annual interest income, against $3,576m of non-GAAP operating income. Base FY2033 non-GAAP EPS is $7.62 including treasury income and $6.49 excluding it, a 15% difference, and the same 15% gap exists in FY2026. A share repurchase is the largest unmodelled capital-allocation choice, it is set to zero identically in all three scenarios, and management has never used it. No case tests the $20.9bn cash balance, 155% of that year's revenue and 23% of today's market capitalisation, so the set cannot bound per-share outcomes.

Each driver was moved on its own inside the base case and the model re-run. Change in FY2033, in $ millions, ranked by the swing in non-GAAP operating income.

Rank Driver Move tested FY2033 revenue FY2033 non-GAAP operating income FY2033 GAAP operating income FY2033 FCF Total swing

The gross-margin mechanism is the second- and fourth-largest driver and it is asymmetric: moving the telemetry wedge four points a year costs $644m of terminal operating income on the downside and earns only $162m on the upside, because the upside runs into the gross-margin cap. Datadog's gross margin has more room to decline than to rise from here, and consensus models it flat. One caveat applies to that pair: the wedge and the unit-cost assumption are not independently identified, because one observed spend increase is split into two unobserved parameters by assuming one of them, so their sensitivities cannot simply be added. Stock compensation is the largest driver of GAAP operating income, a $913m swing, and it does not appear in the non-GAAP line at all — any model that projects only non-GAAP operating income for this company has removed the variable that decides whether it is profitable. The largest customer is a near-term problem, not a terminal-value problem: on FY2027 its ±$100m of ARR is worth $48m of non-GAAP operating income and ranks sixth of eight; by FY2033 it ranks last, worth $60m of a $3,576m line. The FY2027 ranking is different:

FY2027 rank Driver FY2027 swing
1 Gross margin $241m
2 Operating expense intensity $224m
3 Hosting unit cost alone $129m
4 Telemetry wedge alone $111m
5 Base-book retention $57m
6 AI-native cohort $55m
7 Largest customer $48m
8 Stock compensation, non-GAAP line $3m

The terminal year turns on an assumption with no base rate behind it. No member of the software reference class ran a consumption-priced business with a single customer large enough to name in a risk factor, and Snowflake, the closest structural analogue, does not disclose one. The ±10-point move on cohort growth is worth $3.9bn of FY2033 revenue between the ends, 29% of the base-case revenue line.

17.7 Assumptions the evidence does not fully support

Two assumptions do not reproduce and are corrected in Section 17.4. The rest below are where the evidence points somewhere other than the base, with the direction and the size.

Assumption Base Where the evidence points Size
Q3 2026 revenue $1,168m (a +2.5% beat) The empirical distribution says $1,188m, which is the model's bull: 27 of 27 beats at a +4.25% trailing mean in a +3.1% to +5.2% band. The base's +2.46% beat is below the minimum realised beat of the last twelve quarters. Against that, the implied full-year cushion of 3.0-3.6% roughly matches the largest customer's reduction, so the reduction consumes about one year's cushion The bear at $1,138m is a 0-of-27 event and should be labelled as such
Base-book net retention, FY2026 and FY2027 118.5% and 116.0% Decomposing the disclosed low-120s total, with the largest customer at about 200% net expansion and the rest of the cohort at 150%, gives base-book retention nearer 116.4% for FY2026. Two undisclosed methods disagree by about five points; a second method built off the model's own ARR anchors gives about 121% Shift the range down about two points. At $758m of terminal swing per ±2 points, a two-point level error is worth roughly $400m of FY2033 operating income
FY2027 decay in base-book retention 1.5 points Dynatrace decayed about 3 points a year (120%+ to 111%) and Elastic about 3 (117% to 110%). Against that, Datadog is the only one of the three to have run a full decay-and-recovery cycle and neither comparable re-accelerated, so a mechanical decay on a series that has risen for eight quarters is itself unsupported Range should shift to roughly 110.5 / 114.0 / 118.0
New-logo ARR, FY2027 5.0% of opening ARR Every recent disclosure points up: new-logo annualised bookings more than doubled in both Q1 and Q2 2026, average land size set a record, and new customers supplied 30% of the Q2 2026 revenue increase against 25% for FY2025. FY2025's back-solved layer was 6.1%; getting to 5.0% requires new-logo dollars to grow only 11.9% a year while the bookings metric doubled twice Base should sit nearer 5.6-5.8%; the current bull of 6.5% is closer to the evidence
AI-native cohort ex-largest, FY2026 and FY2027 $560m and $868m The FY2026 range is far too narrow at −10.7%/+3.6% on a quantity where every input is an estimate stacked on an estimate. For FY2027, the disclosed year-over-year cohort increment has been essentially flat at $52-66m for five quarters, which is linear, not exponential, and extrapolates to about +40% against +55% FY2026 spread should be at least ±20%; FY2027 base should move toward $780-800m, and the bear at $625m is better supported. On the base path AI-native concentration rises from 13.7% to 16.2% of ARR in the year after the disclosed reduction
AI-native cohort growth, FY2027-33 +19.7% compound The model's number-one sensitivity driver, worth $1,050m of terminal operating income, has no evidence anchor and the justification concedes it. The sharpest problem is the bear: +4.0% compound still grows the cohort 26% cumulatively over six years, so no scenario contains contraction. The closest observed analogue is Datadog's own 2022-23 episode, where growth declined 59 points and sequential growth compressed eightfold in five quarters The base survives only as a stated convention. The bear should reach contraction
Largest customer, FY2026 and FY2027 $120m and $135m The bear at $60m sits below the disclosed floor: Datadog described a nine-figure renewal in the quarter the step-down began and a nine-figure annualized expansion three quarters earlier, and a customer pays its commit whether or not it consumes it. The base at $135m has the account growing 12.5% in the year after a 45% cut, supported only by commit language, while named external views point the other way Raise the bear to about $100m. The line is worth $48m of FY2027 non-GAAP operating income at ±$100m, so a 50% error costs less than a two-point error in the gross-margin build
Hosting unit cost (5)% a year Not independently identified: it is the input that determines the wedge. On the level, non-cancelable purchase commitments went $485.0m to $1,400m in one year, and volume commitments are how hyperscaler unit pricing falls; Snowflake took gross margin from 56% to 67% on entirely rented infrastructure. Against that, the same three counterparties host, take channel margin and sell competing products Midpoint survives; it should not be presented as independent of the wedge, and the terminal margin recovery rests entirely on compounding it for eight years
Non-GAAP gross margin, FY2033 79.3% The rented-cloud observability class settles at 74-79% with a central of about 77%, so the terminal is at or above the top of the band in a business whose gross margin has declined in six of the last ten quarters Terminal is optimistic by roughly 2 points against the class central
Incremental-margin governor 36.2% Calibrated on the single best realised year, so it permits five consecutive years above anything Datadog has sustained. The six-year cumulative realised rate is 24.9% and the base case's cumulative FY2026-33 rate is 28.1%. The right governor is the sustained rate, not the annual maximum As constructed the cap binds in no base or bull year, so it constrains nothing
Stock compensation, FY2026 $875m Second-half compensation exceeded the first half in each of the last two years, at 1.115x and 1.178x; applying those to 1H2026's $417.1m gives $882-909m. The scenario set contains no downside at all, with the bear equal to the base and the bull $5m below Bear should be about $910m. In a year whose base-case GAAP operating income is $76m, a $20-35m understatement is 26-46% of that line
Cash yield, FY2028 onward 3.25% Realised yield was 4.49% in FY2025 and 4.22% annualised in 1H2026, and the only rate evidence available is a 3.753% three-month bill and a 4.449% five-year, with 37% of the portfolio maturing beyond a year. A 3.25% blended yield requires the short end near 2.5%, which nothing cited supports Conservative in direction. 100bp on the FY2033 base balance is $209m, 12% of that year's GAAP operating income
Cash taxes, % of GAAP provision bear 95%, base 60%, bull 70% The ordering is not monotonic and the bull is worse than the base. A higher cash-tax ratio is unambiguously worse for free cash flow, so the bull should be lowest; under the alternative reading, that a more profitable bull consumes loss carryforwards faster, the bear should be lowest. Neither reading makes 95/60/70 coherent The level checks out at $37-49m of FY2027 cash taxes against a FY2026 guide of $30-40m. The ordering should not be taken as intentional
Capex and capitalized software 1.2% and 2.7% of revenue, flat across scenarios Both sit below the most recent actual. Property and equipment was 1.45% of revenue in FY2025; capitalised software rose every year for four years to 2.50% (FY2025) and 2.89% in 1H2026, and the model reverses that. Three disclosed items point up: Datadog announced a UK datacenter, offers cloud-prem deployment, and held $220.9m of not-yet-commenced leases with a 9.0-year term Small in cash terms. The direction matters beyond cash flow, because capitalised software is development cost moved off the operating expense line
Deferred revenue and deferred contract costs 35.5% and 5.7% of revenue Deferred revenue has oscillated in a 33-38% band for seven years with no trend, and the model takes it to 32.5% by FY2033, below the seven-year minimum, while billings grew 38% against revenue up 36% in Q2 2026, which is the condition under which the ratio rises. Deferred contract costs are set below the most recent actual with a bear-to-bull span narrower than a single year's observed move One point of deferred revenue on FY2027 revenue is $56m of one-time cash. Immaterial to conclusions, and the ranges are too narrow
Tuck-in acquisition spend $100m a year Eight times the seven-year median of $12.5m and above five of the seven years. The model also books the cash outflow every year and credits no acquired revenue in any year, so $800m goes out over eight years for nothing Conservatism applied to one side of a transaction. The 50-200 range is defensible against the two step-up years; the base should move toward $60-75m or the model should credit acquired revenue

Eight assumptions were attacked and held:

  • the ARR-to-revenue conversion factor, where the error is 0.4% of a $13.4bn line and runs conservative;
  • net customer adds and the $100k+ and $1m+ ladder projections, each of which is held at the current absolute pace;
  • the FY2033 base-book retention of 108.5%, which is at the bottom of a 108-116% class band and below both comparables' plateau;
  • the FY2033 operating expense intensity of 52.7%, which takes 0.48 points a year against a realised five-year rate of 2.0;
  • the FY2033 stock-compensation intensity, argued above;
  • the convertible settlement at zero new shares;
  • the GAAP tax rate;
  • days sales outstanding.

18. Risks

Risk 1 — AI-native cohort concentration and the unnamed largest customer. High severity, already occurring. Mechanism: revenue is usage-based with only the committed portion ratable, so a single customer's decision to move workloads, renegotiate unit prices or build in-house flows through to revenue within a quarter with no contractual floor beyond its commit. Because the platform prices per host, per container, per GB and per session, a customer that shrinks its fleet shrinks its bill immediately, and the customer belongs to a cohort of the fastest-scaling and least predictable buyers in the economy. Exposure: the cohort was 750 customers at Q2 2026 with 31 above $1m and 8 above $10m, 11% of FY2025 revenue and roughly a third of the FY2025 revenue increase; the largest customer is plausibly $150-300m annualized, 3-7% of run-rate revenue. The Q3 2026 guide implies a sequential add of $18.5m against the $115m just delivered, and the full-year guide embeds a further 3-4 points of deceleration in Q4.

Leading indicators, in order of speed:

  • whether the cohort's percentage-point sentence in the Q3 2026 10-Q drops below the high-single-digit band or is restructured again;
  • whether the "largest customer reduce their usage" sentence persists, becomes plural, or acquires a magnitude;
  • the sequential revenue add against a guide that needs only $18.5m;
  • the net-retention band;
  • the count of AI customers above $1m and $10m.

Mitigation already in place: the customer renewed on a nine-figure contract covering 17 products, guidance was fully de-risked in both Q3 and the full year, the full-year guide has still been raised three times for a cumulative $390m, and gross revenue retention remains mid- to high 90s.

Risk 2 — Gross-margin erosion from third-party cloud hosting. High severity, already occurring. Mechanism: Datadog outsources substantially all infrastructure, so hosting is booked in cost of revenue instead of depreciation, and the gross-margin ceiling is set by the same three parties that sell competing native monitoring. Product launches consume infrastructure before they are optimised and large-customer growth spikes consume it faster than commercial terms adjust. Exposure: 380 basis points of decline from the Q4 2023 peak of 83.4% to 79.6%, worth roughly $169m of gross profit at FY2026 guided revenue, about 17% of the operating income guide. Cost of revenue grew 45% in Q2 2026 against 36% revenue growth, with $64.1m of the $74.1m increase named as hosting. If the current nine-point wedge persists another four quarters, gross margin declines a further ~140 basis points. Leading indicators: the wedge between cost-of-revenue growth and revenue growth in each 10-Q, which is the cleanest single number; whether the MD&A attribution sentence recurs; whether the "80% plus or minus" language survives a second sub-80% print; and capex plus capitalized software as a share of revenue, where a step up would signal a shift toward owned capacity. The cloud-hosting payable line is not a usable indicator — the filings state it swings with invoice timing, and its year-over-year and sequential readings point in opposite directions.

Risk 3 — The hyperscalers occupy four roles at once. High severity, structural. AWS, Azure and GCP are the landlord setting the input cost, named competitors for cloud monitoring, a distribution channel the 10-K says has worse economics, and, as of Q2 2026, customers. Datadog cannot diversify these counterparties, because the platform is built on rented cloud. Datadog has never disclosed the marketplace revenue mix, so this exposure cannot be sized from any filing. Leading indicators: any disclosure of marketplace revenue mix; a change to the competitor list in Item 1; gross margin; whether the hyperscaler-as-customer language recurs.

Risk 4 — Usage-based revenue and customer cost optimization. High severity, base rate established. Broader than Risk 1: consumption pricing transmits any customer efficiency drive directly into revenue, and the 2022-23 episode happened to this company with this pricing model. Revenue growth went from +63% (FY2022) to +27% (FY2023), a 36-point deceleration in one year. Net retention went from above 130% to below 120%. The word "optimiz*" appeared 5-7 times per call before and after and 39 times on the Q2 2023 call. Duration was roughly six quarters from first flagging to moderation. Management draws the relevant distinction, and it is also the reason for caution: "We've seen that movie before… Now of course, the situation is different, like it's a small part of our business today, whereas a very large part of our business was cloud native." The AI cohort was 11% of revenue against a cloud-native cohort that was a plurality of the base in 2022. The FY2025 and prior filings framed the AI cohort as the cloud-native sequel; the Q2 2026 10-Q removed that framing in the same filing that disclosed the reduction.

Risk 5 — Stock-based compensation and dilution. Medium-high severity, continuous. Non-GAAP operating profit is approximately the add-back and GAAP operating economics are negative, so revenue deceleration with flat compensation produces a widening GAAP loss immediately, because grant-date expense does not flex with revenue. Share count grows every year, there is no buyback, and the diluted count is guided from ~372m to ~376m for FY2026 and ~378m for Q3. The mitigant is real and recent: intensity declined to 19.6% of revenue in Q2 2026 from 21.8% a year earlier. Leading indicator: the weighted-average diluted share guidance given each quarter, which moves before the reported figure does.

Risk 6 — Governance: dual-class control plus the Nevada move. Medium severity, structural, recently worsened. Class B holds 42% of voting power on 6.8% of shares, and the April 2026 redomiciliation narrowed the shareholder remedies available against that control: the Delaware business-combination analysis was deleted, exclusive forum moved to Clark County, Nevada, and officer exculpation in derivative actions became available. Concurrent insider 10b5-1 adoptions in the June 2026 quarter, including 1,332,312 shares for the co-founder CTO, were disclosed in the same filing as the largest customer's usage reduction. The offsetting fact is that control is time-limited and the clock is two-thirds run: every Class B share converts in September 2029 and the redomiciliation did not reset that date. Leading indicators: the next proxy's treatment of the Nevada vote; Class B voting power in each 10-Q; Form 4 volume against the adopted plans.

Risk 7 — A reliability and security vendor suffering its own outage or breach. Medium severity, both have happened once. Datadog runs a root-level agent inside customers' production estates and holds their telemetry, logs and security signals, so a compromise reaches the customer base as well as the company. Two realized precedents: the March 2023 multi-region outage, and an April 2025 source-code breach first disclosed in the FY2025 10-K, where "an unauthorized third party" accessed source-code repositories through compromised employee credentials and the filing states the access "may increase our vulnerability to certain attacks at a later date." The surrounding verb also changed from "may" to "have been and in the future." The peer base rate is SolarWinds' 2020 supply-chain compromise, which permanently reset that company's trajectory. Exposure is not sizable from disclosure: Datadog has never disclosed a service-level-agreement credit amount. Leading indicators: whether the April 2025 example is retained, expanded or joined by a second in the next 10-K; any credit disclosure; status-page incident frequency.

Risk 8 — Competition, OpenTelemetry and the stale competitor list. Medium severity, slow-acting. Once a customer's applications emit OpenTelemetry, switching a backend becomes a routing-configuration change instead of a re-instrumentation project, and Datadog's response was to embed the OTel Collector directly in its own agent, which lowers the switching cost in both directions. Datadog made that trade deliberately, and it is still a trade. The EU Data Act, added to Item 1A in FY2025, "introduces new obligations related to data portability and services switching", so a switching-cost issue now arrives as a compliance requirement. The filed competitor list names New Relic (private since November 2023) and SolarWinds (private since April 2025) and omits Grafana Labs and Chronosphere, which are the two names the sell side asks about by name. Three peer failure tests apply differently. New Relic warns about a pricing transition. On the current state Datadog grew 36% against Dynatrace's 16.2% and Elastic's 16.0% in comparable recent quarters. SolarWinds is the security precedent. Splunk is the takeout Datadog is winning, and the mechanism that ended Splunk's independence was priced ingest, which Datadog also prices.

Risk 9 — New customer additions have stalled. Medium severity, early. Land-and-expand needs land, and a stall at the top of the funnel takes years to show in revenue but shows in customer count first. Net adds were +200 in Q2 2026 against a 500-900 range, in a DASH quarter that added 900 a year earlier. Management's explanation is plausible and partly corroborated — the variability sits "at the very low end, the border between free and contract", the $100k+ count rose 4,550 to 4,720 in the quarter, and new-logo annualized bookings more than doubled — and it is also the same explanation given in many quarters, and one quarter at +200 does not settle it.

Risk 10 — Remaining performance obligations have gone flat while revenue accelerated. Low-medium severity, watch item. RPO was flat for two quarters, +0.3% over six months, while revenue grew 34% and billings 38%. Year-over-year RPO is +43% and current RPO about +40%, and both readings are correct. Management's standing position — "we continue to believe revenue is a better indication of our business trends than billing and RPO" — is defensible for a consumption business where much revenue is not ratable, and it is also a standing deflection of the backlog question. Leading indicator: sequential RPO in Q4 2026, the seasonal booking quarter; a flat Q4 would be the signal.

18.1 Which risks fire together

The plausible bad scenario is a combination of items that share one driver, the AI capital-expenditure cycle turning from build to optimize. The largest customer's reduction generalizes across a cohort of 750 members facing the same unit-economics pressure at the same time, which is the 2022-23 mechanism with a different cohort and a base rate of 36 points of deceleration over four quarters. Gross margin keeps compressing. Hosting cost is growing nine points faster than revenue, and if AI-native volume declines, $1.4bn of non-cancelable commitments does not decline with it, so deleveraging committed hosting against falling usage compresses margin faster on the way down than it built on the way up. No one has sized the decline rate at which the $1.4bn commitment binds, or the gross margin that prints there. A competitive price response arrives in the same window, because a demand-side pause is when discounting starts and Datadog's own Flex Logs price cut is the template. The GAAP line gives no headroom, because FY2025 already showed a GAAP operating loss at +28% growth and stock compensation does not flex with revenue. And the 25%+ margin target becomes unreachable, since reaching it requires operating leverage from a base whose gross margin is declining.

A rough shape of the combined case, each input drawn from a disclosed trend extended one year and none of it disclosure: FY2027 revenue growth in the mid-to-high teens against the high-20s the ex-AI base currently implies, non-GAAP gross margin near 77-78%, non-GAAP operating margin stalled at 23%, diluted shares still growing 3%+ a year, and a widening GAAP operating loss. The offsetting case is equally concrete and comes from the same filings: the base excluding AI customers has accelerated five consecutive quarters to high-20s growth, $100k+ customers are 91% of ARR and growing 23%, gross revenue retention is mid- to high 90s, multi-product attach improved on every threshold, and the full-year guide has been raised three times for a cumulative $390m despite the concentration disclosure.

19. Source disclosure

Sources used. Seven Datadog 10-Ks (FY2019-FY2025), six 10-Qs (2024-Q3 and 2025-Q1 through 2026-Q2), 28 earnings-call transcripts covering every post-IPO quarter from Q3 2019 to Q2 2026, 74 presentation transcripts from 2019-12-02 to 2026-06-03 including four analyst and investor days, eight investor decks with 635 slides, 28 EX-99.1 earnings press releases from Q3 2019 onward, which is where the quarterly operating KPIs live, guidance extracts for Q4 2022 through Q2 2026, and eight DEF 14As from 2020-04-24 to 2026-04-29, including the 2026-02-27 special-meeting proxy on the Nevada redomiciliation. Peer filings: Dynatrace and Elastic (six 10-Ks each), Cisco, IBM, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and SolarWinds. Daloopa provided 493 metrics and 5,626 period-values. Bloomberg supplied daily prices and total returns since the IPO, the full BEst consensus grid to FY2030, weekly consensus revision history, peer fundamentals, and the 30-row comparable-company table.

Gaps and failures.

  • No primary broker note is behind the consensus figures. Every consensus figure comes from Bloomberg BEst, and the qualitative street view in Sections 8 and 14 comes from press reporting of broker notes.
  • No pre-computed risk-factor diff exists for Datadog. The seven-year risk-factor delta in Sections 6 and 18 was built by hand from the 10-K text.
  • No 10-Q before 2024-Q3 was used, so the six quarters of the 2022-23 downcycle from Q2 2022 to Q4 2023 are covered only by 10-Ks, press releases and calls. The quarterly MD&A is where cost of revenue and gross margin are explained through a demand slowdown, and it is missing for the 2022-23 episode that several sections build on.
  • No 8-K was used. The 2026-04-22 8-K containing the Plan of Conversion, the Nevada articles and the special-meeting voting results is not reflected here, which is why the Nevada vote tally is unverified. Neither is the August 2019 Form S-1, which holds the FY2016-FY2018 pre-IPO financials the seven-year series truncates.
  • No SEC filings exist for New Relic (private since November 2023), Grafana Labs or Chronosphere, so every figure for those three is a company press release or press report, and New Relic's pre-buyout margin, retention and customer trajectory are not behind the peer-failure comparison in Section 18.
  • No external dataset underlies any figure. No figure carries a [data:] citation.
  • investors.datadoghq.com times out at zero bytes. The August 2026 investor presentation was recovered, but the rest of the investor-relations site — the quarterly results archive, 8-K exhibits, governance documents — was not enumerated.
  • Two web sources returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch (TheStreet and Benzinga) and were read only through search summaries. Both are tagged [web, unverified].
  • No intraday price data, so earnings reactions are close-to-close on the release session. Datadog reports pre-market, so the full session is captured but the opening gap cannot be separated from the day's drift.
  • The 2026-08-10 price is intraday. Every multiple dated 2026-08-10 moves with it; the last settled close was $233.93 on 2026-08-07, at which EV to forward sales was 15.9x against 17.5x.

Discrepancies found and how they were resolved. Where sources disagreed, the figure as printed in the filed consolidated statements won. Eleven disagreements were logged. Daloopa places FY2018 earnings per share and share counts in the FY2019 and FY2020 slots, which was rejected in favour of the filings. The XBRL extraction returns zero for FY2019 basic shares, a stray $32,000 of FY2019 interest expense for a year in which Datadog had no borrowings, and a depreciation figure $6.6m below the cash-flow-statement line; the filings were used throughout. Bloomberg's capital-expenditure field sums purchases of property and equipment with capitalized software, so no peer comparison sourced from Bloomberg should be set against Datadog's $49.6m property line alone. Bloomberg's EBITDA differs from the definition used here (GAAP operating income plus depreciation and amortization) by an unpublished reconciliation, so the two must not be mixed. FY2019 non-GAAP operating income is unresolved: the Q4 2019 release reports $(5.4)m and the Q4 2020 release restates it to $(3.9)m, neither ties to GAAP operating income plus stock compensation, and the definition changed between the two releases without explanation — so FY2019 is shown as not disclosed and the reproducible $(1.1)m stock-comp-excluded figure is used instead. The FY2020 count of customers above $1m of ARR was reported as 97 and restated to 101 a year later. The Q4 2025 release and the 10-K differ by 1,000 shares on the diluted count and by $1 thousand on full-year non-GAAP operating income. Two filings disagree on FY2025 contractual interest expense, at zero in the 10-K and $364k for the first half in the 10-Q. Everything else — revenue, gross profit, operating income, net income, diluted EPS, operating cash flow, free cash flow and gross margin — ties exactly across the filings, XBRL and Bloomberg for every year and every quarter.

Internal inconsistencies. Six internal disagreements, each named with both values and with the figure used elsewhere.

  • Market capitalisation against share count. The front-matter table prints $92,632m of market capitalisation beside 358,956,785 shares and a $257.26 price, but those two multiply to $92,345m; $92,632m implies 360.1m shares, which is the count Bloomberg used for the Section 16 table as well. Every multiple in the dossier follows from the $88,924m enterprise value the larger count produces.
  • The 2026-08-10 price. $257.26 in the front matter and Section 15, $257.08 in the Section 16 Bloomberg pull, and $256.50 in the Section 12.2 conversion and capped-call arithmetic. All three are intraday reads of the same session; $257.26 is the figure the rest of the document uses.
  • Net cash. $(3,708)m in the front-matter capitalisation table against $3,985.4m in Section 12.1, which is total liquidity less note principal at the same date. The $277m gap is not explained anywhere; Section 12.1 is the balance-sheet measure and the front-matter figure is the one embedded in enterprise value and every multiple.
  • AI-native cohort size at Q2 2026. $149-165m a quarter in Section 1.6 against $149-174m in Section 6.1, because the two readings put the top of "high single digit percentage points" at 9 and at 10 points respectively. The lower bound and the method are identical.
  • Acquisition consideration in the first half of 2026. Section 11.2 records $75.3m of restricted shares issued, while the $191.5m aggregate less $98.5m of net cash and $14.3m of deferred holdback leaves $78.7m, which is also what the $98.80 implied issue price on 796,509 shares produces. The 10-Q business-combination note would settle it.
  • The 2024 dilution-target slide. The Appendix A caption reports actual dilution of 1.7-2.4% for 2020-2023 as plotted on the slide, against 1.86-3.72% computed on ending shares in Section 12.4. Management has never stated which share basis its target uses, which is the likely cause and is not confirmed.

20. What we still don't know, and the metrics that would resolve it

20.1 Unresolved gaps that limit conclusions in this dossier

  1. International is 29% of revenue and the only major dimension decelerating. International revenue was $994m in FY2025, larger than the whole Log Management pillar, growing 22.7% against North America's 29.8% and declining to 27% of first-half 2026 revenue. No EMEA or APAC split exists anywhere in the corpus beyond the regional ARR pie in the 2026 deck and a Latin America series showing $7m to $155m. One consolidated retention rate and one new-logo rate cover a business where 71% grows 38% and 29% grows 24% and decelerating.
  2. Currency is quantified on neither side of the profit and loss account. Revenue is billed by customer address across 160-plus countries while 44% of roughly 8,100 employees are outside the United States and 34% of those in France, and the Q2 2026 10-Q disclosed active foreign-exchange forwards designated as cash-flow hedges for the first time, with management conceding "limited experience establishing hedging programs". Whether the international deceleration is translation or demand is unresolved, and a euro-heavy cost base is unmodelled inside the operating-expense path that is Section 17's second-largest near-term sensitivity.
  3. Datadog discloses almost nothing about the customer base below $100k of ARR or the funnel that feeds it. 28,390 customers hold about 10% of ARR at roughly $13.6k each, and quarterly net adds declined to +200. There is no trial-to-paid funnel data, no commercial-versus-enterprise split of the customer count beyond the deck's statement that 72% of $100k+ customers are commercial accounts, with the rest enterprise-field, and nothing that would test management's free-versus-contract-boundary explanation. Section 17's new-logo assumption, worth a $568m terminal swing, has no funnel evidence behind it.
  4. Sales-force productivity is not disclosed. Enterprise account executives grew from about 458 to about 600 in 2025, up 31%, while enterprise average ARR went from about $490k to about $505k, up 3%, and net adds declined sharply. The only customer-acquisition-payback datapoint Datadog has ever published is a 2021 deck slide showing about 7 months against 12-44 months for four unnamed competitors, and it stopped publishing it. Section 17 assumes sales and marketing leverage from 23% toward 19-20% of revenue with no efficiency evidence behind it.
  5. Software Delivery is the largest claimed market slice and has no disclosed revenue. The 2026 deck puts it at roughly $41bn of the roughly $116bn stacked opportunity, larger than observability and larger than security, and it is the one major product area with no ARR chart in the deck. Section 4's market sizing and the model's post-FY2029 growth lean on new-product ramps whose largest claimed adjacency has no sized revenue, growth rate or attach evidence anywhere.
  6. Customer industry mix is unknown. The 10-K carries no vertical split, and the deck's top-ten-by-vertical penetration slide is a logo statistic. Whether the accelerating non-AI-native base is itself concentrated in internet, software and payments customers whose spending tracks the same AI capital cycle is unasked and unanswered — and it matters more than it looks, because roughly 72% of ARR already sits with customers running AI integrations.
  7. What the ex-AI-native growth rate is made of. The series 18% → 20% → 23% → mid-20s → high-20s offsets much of the AI-cohort risk, and it is a spoken rounded band that appears in no filing and reconciles to no disclosed line. The cohort definition changed mid-series when Q2 2026 added hyperscaler in-house AI labs, with no statement of restatement. How much of the ten points of acceleration is reclassification and how much is demand is unknown. If two points are definitional, Section 7's ranking, Section 8's concentration answer and Section 17's reverse-engineered base-book retention all move.
  8. Whether the non-AI-native base is insulated from the AI cycle at all. The deck discloses that customers running AI integrations held about 45% of ARR in 2023, about 62% in 2024 and about 72% in 2025. The dossier presents AI-native and non-AI-native as separate lines because that is how the company discloses them, and the company's own slide says roughly 72% of ARR sits with AI-integrated customers.
  9. The hyperscaler beta is in no forward view. AWS grew +37% in Q2 2026 against Datadog's +35.6%, the first time in the company's public life, and the measured asymmetry is 2.30 points of Datadog deceleration per point of AWS deceleration against 0.46 on the way up. Neither Bloomberg consensus nor the model in Section 17 contains any hyperscaler linkage. A 2.3x downside beta against a hyperscaler retracing from +37% toward +20% is a worse case than the modelled FY2027 bear of +15.9%.
  10. What an incremental engineer buys, and whether Datadog can keep them. Section 3's conclusion depends on research spend at 45.2% of revenue and 3.3x the nearest pure-play, with the CTO locating the asset in a proprietary eval corpus that "you can't outsource to nonexperts." Datadog discloses nothing on attrition, engineer retention, culture, or compensation competitiveness against the labs hiring the same people, and nothing on the concentration of 44% of employees outside the United States with a third of those in one country. The $2,078.3m of unrecognised stock compensation over 2.8 years that is the retention mechanism is analysed only as a committed accounting floor.
  11. What gross margin does when usage declines. The $1.4bn commitment covers roughly half to three-quarters of consumption and usage would have to fall substantially before it binds. At what rate of decline it binds, and what gross margin prints there, is unbuilt; Section 18.1 names it without quantifying it.
  12. The ARR concentration inside the large-customer tail. 603 customers at $1m+ hold an estimated 56-66% of total ARR and 34 customers above $10m hold at least 8%, and neither figure reaches the risk framework, which treats concentration as a one-customer problem, or the model, which splits ARR three ways with no tail structure.

20.2 Open questions and the metric that would resolve each

Question What would resolve it
What is the largest customer's actual annualized revenue, and what is the post-renewal commit level? A customer-concentration disclosure at 10% of revenue, or the total contract value and term of the nine-figure renewal. Neither is disclosed
Does "fully derisked" mean the guide contains only the contractual commit, with all usage above it as upside? Management's commit language implies it and it is not confirmed. The Q3 2026 print settles it: a beat of the usual size says the de-risking was conservative
What is total ARR? A single disclosed figure would collapse roughly half the estimates in this dossier to disclosure
What is the invoicing lag on the cloud-hosting payable? It decides whether the total cloud bill is 11% or 29% of revenue, and therefore how much cloud cost is above the gross-margin line
What share of revenue flows through cloud-provider marketplaces, and at what take rate? The 10-K has flagged margin compression from this channel in identical language for seven years and has never sized it. The deck gives 15% of ARR as channel-influenced without separating marketplace from reseller
Is the largest customer above or below the corporate average gross margin? Testable at the Q3 2026 print: gross margin rising while revenue growth decelerates would confirm that the step-down is margin-accretive, and would mean the street's second-half recovery happens for a reason nobody has articulated
What share of customers instrument via OpenTelemetry instead of the Datadog agent? Never disclosed in any filing, call or deck, and without it the OpenTelemetry exposure cannot be sized. Package-download trend data is the only external proxy available (Appendix C)
What is gross retention by product count, in numbers? The 2026 deck plots it without printing the values. This is the number that would settle whether the unified data model creates switching cost or merely correlates with customer sophistication
What is Datadog's win rate against Grafana Cloud, Chronosphere and hyperscaler-native tooling? Never disclosed, and the single most decision-relevant unknown for the moat
Why did new-logo additions halve in the first half of 2026? Deliberate up-market repositioning, saturation at the small end, or share loss at the low-ARPU end. The disclosure does not distinguish them; two more quarters of net adds at 200-300 alongside decelerating $100k+ growth would
Did Flex Logs cross $100m of ARR? Last disclosed as "nearing $100 million" at Q4 2025 and not updated on either 2026 call
Has the board considered a repurchase? Against $3,985m of net cash, 3%-plus annual dilution and a base case accumulating $20.9bn of cash by FY2033, this is the largest single item the model leaves out. The 2026 investor-day capital-allocation answer named organic investment and M&A only
Will the 2029 notes principal be settled in cash? Management has never stated an intention. The answer moves real dilution by roughly 3.9m shares
What did the three FY2025 and three 1H2026 acquisitions actually buy, and which counterparties are the three unnamed deals? No filing names a target for any of them, and three post-IPO deals are unnamed in every available source
Why did remaining performance obligations decline sequentially in a quarter containing a nine-figure renewal? Either the renewal was executed after 30 June or it replaced a larger prior commitment. Nothing reconciles it
Why did non-cancelable purchase commitments step 2.9x in one year, and who is the counterparty? No filing or transcript explains the renegotiation, and the 10-Q refers to "our third-party cloud infrastructure provider costs" in the singular without naming anyone
What is the credit-rating distribution inside the $3,793m of corporate credit? Not disclosed anywhere, on a portfolio that produced 159% of FY2025 GAAP net income

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

What eight investor decks and 635 slides add that the filings and transcripts do not, each cross-referenced to the body section it also informs.

  • Product-line economics exist only in the decks. Log Management ARR grew about 7x from roughly $145m (2020) to $1.0bn (2025) with growth troughing near 25% in 2024 and re-accelerating to about 29% as Flex Logs scaled; Digital Experience Monitoring reached roughly $290m, split about $170m Real User Monitoring, $110m Synthetics and $10m Product Analytics; and the "APM crossed $1bn" milestone is APM plus DEM, so core APM with profiling and database monitoring is about $0.7bn. No filing contains any of this. (§1, §2)
  • The security business is roughly $107m of ARR against a claimed $30bn market slice. The suite grew from about $4m (2020) to about $107m (2025), roughly 2.6% of ARR, and Datadog says as much itself on the next slide: 70% of $1m+ customers use a security product and security is 2% of those customers' spend. Broad adoption, negligible wallet share. (§4)
  • The pricing model is shown as engineered deflation. At one enterprise customer, indexed-log volume rose about 75x while unit price declined, producing about 4x revenue, so unit price is roughly 5% of its 2021 level. Revenue growth on this line requires volume to outrun deliberate price reduction. (§1, §3)
  • Gross retention by product count, plotted and unlabelled. Roughly 87% at one to two products rising to about 99% at ten or more. The company-wide "mid- to high 90s" is a blend of two very different businesses, and the company figure will drift up mechanically as product count rises. This is the disclosed evidence behind the switching-cost argument. (§2, §3)
  • The AI-native cohort's revenue share, which the calls stopped publishing. 1% (2021), 1%, 2%, 5%, 11% (2025), which applied to reported revenue means the cohort supplied roughly a third of the FY2025 revenue increase. (§1, §6)
  • The AI exposure is far wider than that cohort. The share of ARR held by customers running AI integrations went from about 45% (2023) to about 62% (2024) to about 72% (2025). (§1, §6, §20)
  • A customer tier the filings never report. Customers above $10m of ARR went 3 (2020) → 34 (2025), a 63% compound rate, so at least $340m of ARR sits with 0.1% of accounts. (§1, §7)
  • Added ARR by type, which reframes the platform argument. New customers declined to about 26% of ARR added in 2025 from about 44% in 2023, expansion inside existing products rose to about 57%, and cross-sell of new products has been flat in an 11-21% band for six years while the product count tripled. (§6)
  • Enterprise land size and installed-base average moved in opposite directions in 2025. Average land ARR rose roughly 70% to about $85k after five years of ~15% increments, while enterprise average ARR was nearly flat at about $505k after four years of 25-45% growth. Much bigger new deals, a stalled installed-base average. (§4, §20)
  • Channel-influenced ARR is sized in the deck and nowhere else, at 4% of ARR in 2020 rising to 15% in 2025 — roughly $600m running through partners and hyperscaler marketplaces, against a 10-K that has flagged the margin effect in identical language for seven years without sizing it. (§3, §5)
  • Research spend against the independent peer set. Roughly $970m non-GAAP for Datadog on a trailing basis against about $305m and $285m for the two remaining independents, and a third peer that disappears from the chart after 2023, consistent with the independent observability peer set shrinking by one. (§3)
  • The observability market Datadog quotes was halved between decks, from about $53bn (May 2025) to $28bn (February 2026), by switching the underlying Gartner category, with the 14% market-share statistic computed on the new smaller base. On the old definition the share would be roughly 6-7%. At the same time the total opportunity was restacked to roughly $116bn (2025E) and $185bn (2029E), with Software Delivery now the largest slice. (§4)
  • The addressable account universe shrank from more than 530,000 (February 2024) to more than 470,000 (February 2026) with no explanation, so the improvement in stated logo penetration from 5% to 7% is partly a smaller denominator. (§4, §5)
  • Cohort multiples were restated upward without a note, most sharply the 2019 vintage from 4.4x to 9.7x while other cohorts added 25-35%, and 2019 is the vintage in which the large AI-native accounts landed. (§5)
  • Customer-acquisition payback was published once and never again, at about 7 months against 12-44 months for four unnamed competitors in the 2021 deck. (§20)
  • Two of the three ARR pillars began as acquisitions, per the 2022 deck: acquisitions accelerated time to market in five of sixteen generally available products, including Log Management (2017) and Synthetics (2018). (§11)
  • The margin record against the 25%+ goal, in the company's own table. Hit once, in 2024, declining to 22% in 2025, and FY2026 guidance implies about 22.9%. Research spend has run at 30% of revenue against the 22-26% IPO-era goal. (§14)
  • Two disclosures that quietly disappeared. The 2024 deck's consolidation statistic — "~55% of $1M+ deals in 2023 involve consolidation from competitors" with "~4x higher annualized bookings growth in deals with consolidation" — has no 2026 equivalent. Neither does the international revenue time series, replaced by a single-date regional pie. (§4, §6)
  • Every customer return figure in the deck set is a customer self-report, labelled "based on information provided by the customer and Datadog internal analysis", and every competitive chart uses anonymised "Company 1/2/3/4" labels. Grafana, Chronosphere, Splunk, New Relic, Dynatrace and Elastic are never named in any of the eight decks. (§5)

Appendix C — External data sources

Six external datasets are available for this company. None is used above, and all six are mosaic sources, partial and not comprehensive.

1. Web technology and CDN adoption share — W3Techs, BuiltWith and HTTP Archive. What it measures: the share of public and top-ranked websites running a named vendor's product over time. What it would inform: an external, vendor-independent measure of whether Datadog is gaining or losing share against Dynatrace, Elastic, Grafana and the hyperscaler-native tools, which Section 4 currently answers only from vendor-published ARR figures and an estimated Gartner denominator. It would also give an independent check on the share-gain decomposition in Section 6.2, which currently depends on chart-read market values. Strengthens §4, §3 and §6. 2. Developer-ecosystem adoption — npm and PyPI download trends, GitHub activity, developer surveys. What it measures: adoption and momentum of a vendor's SDK, agent and command-line tooling among developers, by package download trend against competing runtimes, repository activity, and survey usage. What it would inform: the single highest-value item on this list for this company. Section 2.2 identifies the share of customers instrumenting via OpenTelemetry instead of the Datadog agent as the number that would size the OpenTelemetry exposure, and Datadog does not disclose it. The relative download trend of dd-trace packages against OpenTelemetry SDK packages is the only available external proxy, and it would also bear directly on Section 3's conclusion that the moat is at layers three and four, not at collection. Strengthens §2, §1 and §6. 3. Search-interest trends — Google Trends. What it measures: relative search interest for the company and its named products over time and against named peers on a common query basis. What it would inform: a mindshare proxy for the developer-brand position Section 3.5 identifies as the reason the free-trial motion works, and an independent cross-check on the Grafana and Chronosphere momentum in Section 4.4, which currently rests entirely on company press releases. Strengthens §6, §1 and §4. 4. Hiring and headcount signals — job postings, LinkedIn, layoff trackers. What it measures: open-role counts by function, especially go-to-market against engineering, the total posting trend, and any headcount or restructuring actions. What it would inform: two gaps named in Section 20. Sales-force productivity is not computable from disclosure, and Section 17's sales-and-marketing leverage assumption has no efficiency evidence behind it; a posting-mix series would show whether go-to-market hiring is accelerating into the weak logo count. It would also bear on the engineer-retention question, which is unexamined despite Section 3's moat conclusion depending on research spend and a proprietary eval corpus. Strengthens §1, §18 and §10. 5. Service reliability and outage incidents — status pages, post-mortems, Downdetector. What it measures: the frequency, duration and stated root cause of outages over time, and whether they are self-inflicted or third-party. What it would inform: Risk 7 has only two realized precedents behind it — the March 2023 outage and the April 2025 source-code breach — with no series behind them, and Datadog has never disclosed a service-level-agreement credit amount. An incident-frequency series would put a base rate under a risk that is currently two datapoints, and Section 9's finding that the 2023 outage produced no measurable commercial consequence would gain or lose weight against it. Strengthens §18 and §3. 6. Internet traffic and usage telemetry — Cloudflare Radar, Similarweb. What it measures: third-party telemetry on internet and application traffic, bot and AI-crawler share, and product usage. What it would inform: the ultimate exposure in Section 1.5's Driver 1 is the count of billable compute units customers provision, and the only proxies used are hyperscaler revenue and capital-expenditure guidance, which are quarterly and lagged. Traffic and AI-crawler telemetry is higher-frequency and would give an independent measure of the workload growth that drives the telemetry volume Section 17 models as its second-largest sensitivity. Strengthens §6, §1 and §4.
